comment: Absolutely ban personalized pricing without qualification. Allowing it would be bad for society and a nightmare for consumers. It's bad enough that companies have so much unauthorized personal, private data about people, which is already being abused in countless ways. Personalized pricing would weaponize it even more. Naive young people, uneducated and poor people with limited access to information, and trusting seniors would be especially vulnerable to being mislead and abused by personalized pricing.

I believe fair and transparent pricing is key to maintaining a fair market. It also aids in competition. 
With the exit of Spirit Airlines, I would be interested in whether the requirement of displaying pricing influences might cause airline prices to stabilize/drop.

It's absolutely ridiculous and should be considered discrimination that one person can be charged something for an item that someone else is getting charged more money for without even knowing it. There's a difference between negotiating a better price with a car dealer and going to the grocery store to pick up a can of soup. Because everything now is being pushed online if something isn't done about this now companies are going to be using data they already steal from people due to the lack of privacy laws in this country, including peoples bank account information, to then charge people rates based on how much money they make. It also means people who support whatever political party is in power can find that they get special pricing benefits; this is turning into communism. The system going to be abused in so many ways if these companies are allowed to price things individually based off of a consumers individual data.

Personalized pricing should be banned. There is no way that this unfair and abusive mechanism can be waived away merely by warning. Many consumers have no options, so being warned that personalized pricing is in effect when there's no choice is useless. The only solution is to ban this practice.
Absolutely ban personalized pricing. It is an egregious affront to consumer privacy and protections.

I support this enforcement policy that would require businesses to reveal if they are using personalized pricing and what data is being collected to determine prices. Additionally, I support the wholesale ban of personalized pricing AND personalized pay, especially in regards to services like Uber, Lyft, Door Dash, GrubHub, etc. Not only is personalized and algorithmic pricing is used for consumers, but algorithmic pay is being used for workers as well. A picky Uber driver who doesn't take any job will tend to get higher paying rides, while a more desparate, lower-income driver will be shown, algorithmically, lower-priced rides in order to maximize profits for the company.
Very unfair practice. Should be illegal.

Re: Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing, Docket No. FTC-2026-1057

I submit this as an individual consumer. I am not affiliated with any company that does personalized pricing, and no one is paying me to file this.

I am not defending the conduct in the Commission's examples. Charging more for a hotel room because data suggests someone is traveling to a funeral, or more for milk because a household has children, or more for a security camera because someone was recently robbed, is predatory. I would support the Commission going after all of it, hard.

My concern is that this Proposed Statement will not accomplish that, and may make things worse for consumers like me. I have six objections.

1. Disclosure legitimizes the practice instead of stopping it.

The remedy proposed is that companies disclose personalized pricing rather than stop it. Applied to the Commission's own examples, that produces an absurd result: a hotel posting "this price is higher because our data indicates you are traveling for a funeral" would apparently comply. Footnote 20 admits the Commission has not decided whether that conduct is unfair even when disclosed. The document describes conduct that outrages people, then offers a remedy that permits it with a notice attached. I do not want a disclosure. I want the practice prohibited where it is clearly exploitative.

2. The disclosure will not inform me, because none of them do.

I have never read a cookie banner or a privacy policy, and neither has anyone I know. The Commission proposes that companies disclose "the basis for that personalization and the types of data on which the personalization is based" at the moment a price is shown. In practice that is a dense paragraph I will click past like every other notice, and the company will have met its obligation. That is a compliance checkbox, not consumer protection.

3. What I actually want is an opt-out, and it is not in here.

The Commission says the purpose of disclosure is to let consumers "take steps to avoid the higher prices." But the Proposed Statement never requires companies to offer any way to do that. Telling me my price is personalized while giving me no way to turn it off leaves me exactly where I started. I would ask the Commission to require a simple, working opt-out to a standard non-personalized price. That one requirement would do more for consumers than every disclosure in this document combined.

4. The undefined scope threatens discounts I actually use.

Nowhere does the Commission define "personalized pricing." The operative phrase is prices that "vary based on their personal data." That covers my grocery loyalty card, emailed coupons, and app-only prices. Those save me money. If businesses cannot tell which practices are covered, the safe response is to stop personalizing altogether, and the first thing to disappear will be the discounts, not the surcharges. Please state explicitly that loyalty and membership pricing, coupons, promotional codes, and randomized price testing are outside the scope.

5. The Commission has not established what consumers actually expect.

The deception theory rests on the claim that consumers reasonably expect prices not to vary by person. I do not hold that expectation, having shopped at stores where the shelf tag openly displays a member price and a non-member price. The research cited measures whether people think personalized pricing is fair, which is a different question from whether they expected it. The Commission should test the premise by asking consumers before building enforcement on it.

6. The Commission admits it does not know the effects.

The Proposed Statement says the extent of personalized pricing "is not well understood" and its effects "are unclear," and cites research calling the welfare effects "ambiguous and thus a matter of empirical measurement." I take the Commission at its word, and that is my point. That describes something needing study, not a basis for announcing that conduct is likely unlawful.

What I am asking for:

- Prohibit outright the use of data indicating vulnerability, illness, bereavement, disability, or emergency to raise prices. Do not make it disclosable. Make it illegal.
- Require a functioning opt-out to a standard price, not just a notice.
- Define personalized pricing, and exclude loyalty pricing, coupons, and promotional discounts so consumers do not lose them.
- Conduct a 6(b) study and real consumer-perception research before enforcing.
- Resolve the question left open in footnote 20 before this takes effect.

I appreciate the Commission taking this issue up. I am asking it to write the narrow, strong rule instead of the broad, weak one.

Respectfully submitted,

Jesse Shettleroe

The excuse that this lets budget travelers “pay only for what they use” doesn’t hold up when basic things like a carry-on or a assigned seat have quietly become “extras.” Airlines aren’t offering optional luxuries — they’re carving mandatory costs out of the base fare and calling it choice. Meanwhile the psychological trick is well known in the industry: once someone’s 10 minutes into a booking flow, they rarely walk away over a $40 surprise fee, even if they would’ve picked a different airline had they seen the real price upfront.

This isn’t free-market pricing flexibility. It’s a deliberate strategy to win the click with a fake low number and extract the real price after the customer is already committed. Full transparency — one price, all fees included, before checkout — is the bare minimum standard other industries are held to. Airlines fighting that tooth and nail tells you exactly whose interest they’re protecting.

Subject: Complaint Regarding Airline Fee Practices and Declining Passenger Comfort/Value

To the U.S. Department of Transportation, Office of Aviation Consumer Protection:

I am writing to file a formal complaint regarding the current practices of U.S. airlines related to pricing transparency, escalating ancillary fees, and the corresponding decline in passenger comfort and service quality.

Fee Concerns:
Airlines routinely advertise low base fares that do not reflect the actual cost of travel. By the time mandatory or near-mandatory fees are added — for carry-on bags, seat selection, and other items that were once included in the ticket price — the final cost is often significantly higher than the advertised fare. This practice misleads consumers and makes genuine price comparison across airlines difficult or impossible at the point of search.

Value and Comfort Concerns:
At the same time these fees have increased, seat pitch and width have shrunk, legroom has decreased, and basic amenities once included in the fare (snacks, checked bags, seat assignments) have been stripped out and resold as add-ons. Passengers are effectively paying more for less — higher total costs paired with a materially reduced level of comfort and service compared to prior years.

Requested Action:
I urge the Department to:

 1. Enforce and strengthen upfront, all-in fee disclosure requirements at the point of search, before a consumer begins the booking process
 2. Investigate whether current fee structures constitute deceptive pricing practices
 3. Consider minimum standards for seat pitch/width or other passenger comfort protections, given that shrinking space has coincided with rising total travel costs

As a paying consumer, I should be able to see the true, total cost of my ticket before I commit to a purchase, and I should not be expected to accept declining physical comfort as the tradeoff for fees that continue to rise.

Thank you for your attention to this matter

My name is Blake Hunter Yagman, I am the managing attorney and principal of YAGMAN PLLC - a plaintiffs litigation boutique which challenges corporate malfeasance in courtrooms across the country. 

My firm filed the first ever surveillance pricing case against JetBlue Airways, as well as the first ever surveillance wage fixing case against Uber. I was also responsible for helping to prepare the Senate Judiciary Committee for its investigatory hearing on dynamic and surveillance pricing. 

For years, companies have weaponized consumer data against their own consumers. This started with the differentiation of pricing in catalogues and persisted, becoming more advanced, into the digital age. The harms are two-fold: (1) different pricing and price discrimination for individuals seeking to purchase the same goods and services or looking to perform the same type of labor and (2) the privacy related harms associated with the mass surveillance and surreptitious data collection needed to power the surveillance pricing apparatus. 

It is imperative that we protect both consumer and labor rights, as well as privacy rights, which are fundamental legal cornerstones in an age where the use and sale of personal data is the secondary practice of every corporation. The Federal Trade Commission has an obligation to ensure that Section 5 of the FTC Act protects the rights of Americans vulnerable to data that they generally never know is being collected. 

Respectfully Submitted,

Blake Hunter Yagman
The public deserve all prices be set and equal for all people. The use of private should be restricted and not used to determine pricing.

The Commission's intent is misguided.

Price discrimination, although perhaps unpleasant to the ear of some, is a long-recognized economic tool observed in in any robust retail market. Price discrimination is a basic form of personalized pricing that allows sellers to offer discounts to customers who are otherwise less likely to purchase while still maintaining a price above the marginal cost of production. A coupon (whether targeted or made available all), a rebate, even a weekly sale are all forms of price discrimination, often discriminating in favor of the buyer willing to make the extra effort to utilize the discount.

The Commission errs when it seeks to restrict the actions of free actors in the market based on what the Commission decides consumers reasonably expect. The long-established norm the Commission must recognize is that sellers may use any legally obtained information to set prices in their best interest, and buyers may and should be encouraged to do the same. The Commission may encourage consumers to take economic classes, but they must not require sellers to teach them at every checkout opportunity. The example provided in section III, in which the Commission indicates a straightforward indication of personalized pricing would be insufficient because does not contain an unspecified amount of information, suggests the Commission intends to apply a standard to online purchases not currently applied to the price discrimination examples given above.

The Commission should not shape the future of commerce. Governments do consumers no favors by seeking to restrict prices or commerce in general. The Commission must not seek to prohibit personalized pricing of any sort without highly specific evidence of significant harm that outweighs a benefit to the overall market. The theoretical examples provided do not meet this standard and are generally not examples of consumers being vulnerable to personalized pricing but rather of consumers being vulnerable to a lack of competition. The Commission should encourage removal of barriers to entry in these markets rather than making it more costly and more risky for companies to operate in them.

I am submitting this comment to urge the FTC to scrutinize, regulate, and make illegal personalized pricing—the practice of charging consumers different prices for identical products based on data-driven predictions of their willingness to pay.

This practice undermines fair markets by replacing transparent pricing with hidden, data-driven discrimination between buyers. Consumers cannot verify whether they are receiving a fair price, eroding trust in commerce. Those with less time, technical literacy, or resources to detect and circumvent these practices bear a disproportionate burden. Moreover, because pricing algorithms often rely on data correlated with race, gender, age, or geography, personalized pricing risks reproducing discriminatory outcomes even absent explicit intent, potentially violating consumer protection and anti-discrimination principles.

I respectfully urge the agency to require transparency in algorithmic pricing practices and to investigate whether current personalized pricing practices violate existing consumer protection standards.

Respectfully submitted.

This reminds me of how socialists want to tax the rich but instead this will let stores tax them instead while providing no relief to the less wealthy.

What is the point of trying to build a stable financial life if the cost of goods and services is no longer tied to a broader market, but to a single person? This practice takes the idea of progressive taxation and flips it into progressive price setting, benefitting corporations over communities. It’s ridiculous that this is an acceptable practice.

Taking advantage of demographic and other types of data to charge one person
more for the same product, to me, seems very devious. This is especially true when
for personal reasons, someone is very dependent on that product or service, compared to 
the general population. The FTC should be on the side of ordinary residents to ensure that
everyone be treated fairly and equally. Companies should be allowed to make a fair profit,
but should not be allowed to organize a scheme designed to take advantage of one customer
over an another.
Personalized pricing is ultimately a deceptive trade practice that allows unmitigated manipulation of the consumer and creates an unfair approach to retail.
I am against the use of “ Personalized Pricing” and it must be stopped. It is unconstitutional!

I find it totally reprehensible that the government would allow Personalized Pricing. Please put an end to this intrusion into our private lives.
Sincerely,
Diane Knight

The concept of personalized pricing is abhorrent and you should not allow it in any way, shape, or form. It is capitalism unchecked and companies will absolutely take full advantage of hard working families. Do not allow this to happen.

There is a significant difference in stated prices and negotiated prices. 

In negotiated prices, both parties have the opportunity to come to a point of willing buyer and willing seller. Government should not interfere with this as government simply does not have sufficient information to be involved at all. 

If someone states a price in a public setting, people should be assured that everyone will be required to pay that price, or informed otherwise. Changing the price based on conjured information about the prospective buyer is akin to a fraudulent misrepresentation by the seller designed to trick the buyer into believing the lie that everyone pays this price. If the seller wants to engage in this price manipulation the government should not stop it, rather the seller should be required to post their flexible price as a "buy it now" price and give the buyer the opportunity to offer a lower price, thereby creating an honest negotiation on price.
Personalized pricing is disgusting and anything done to make it less common or at least more open has my full support

The commenter who maintains that "The Commission errs when it seeks to restrict the actions of free actors in the market" is saying, in effect, wolves should be allowed to wear sheep's clothing, because there's no law against it, and sheep should know that grazing is risky.

I disagree heartily, and wish the commission had more regulatory authority, not less. The wolves already have a grossly unfair advantage. They don't need protecting, and their predation needs to be curbed.
Insane, greedy, and completely unfair practice.

I believe the FTC may have the authority to prohibit personalized pricing where the pricing can be found to have been on the basis of any protected status of the consumer (race, color, sex, gender, religion, national origin, disability, or age). There may be other avenues to prohibit so called "surveillance pricing" within the scope of federal law, when the data used to inform the pricing decision violates either the privacy act or HIPAA. Additionally, there may be prohibitions built into banking regulations to prevent the use of purchase data (either credit or debit card transaction data) in pricing decisions. Together, a strategy of federal regulation may be achieved by which companies will decide the compliance and liability risks are too great to continue this obviously discriminatory behavior.

I am writing to urge the Federal Communications Commission to prohibit the use of personalized, surveillance-based pricing across broadband, telecommunications, and digital services. Algorithmic price discrimination exploits personal consumer data—such as browsing history, device type, geographic location, and perceived willingness to pay—to charge different consumers different rates for the exact same essential connectivity. This practice undermines market transparency, disproportionately penalizes low-income and vulnerable communities with higher costs, and turns routine consumer data collection into an extractive pricing weapon. Broadband and telecommunications services are fundamental utilities in the modern economy, not luxury commodities to be auctioned off based on behavioral tracking; the FCC must establish clear regulatory safeguards that require transparent, non-discriminatory pricing across the industry.

But the app is a data sponge, soaking up personal information to generate the max price a person in willing to pay. Its creepy, unfair, and should be banned. I understand there can be regional differences between prices, but two people in the same city should not get two different prices for the same product. It seems to me that once an increase has been imposed, it will NEVER decrease back to its original price. If a legitimate effort is made to flex the pricing, not just always increase it, the concept of personalized pricing has merit. But I sadly suspect, like all other marketable products and services, once the price is increased it will remain at that level until another opportunity appears to further increase the cost. I oppose this concept in its expected form.

I hope you can do something about this. The consumer / American citizen is getting squeezed in every direction. Our government needs to help when they can. This should be one of those times. Thank you.

The FTC should absolutely regulate personalized pricing schemes. At the very least, sellers who use this pricing technique should be required to disclose at the point of sale the distributions of sale prices offered and accepted so that consumers can have the information necessary to make rational economic decisions. Capitalism works best when information flow is maximized. The problem with “covert” pricing schemes like this is that the consumer doesn’t know when they’re being fleeced or rewarded. Yes, it’s extra trouble to provide this information, but if a seller has the resources to use this pricing technique, they have the resources to keep track of offers and acceptances, and make those available to prospective buyers. This way, you preserve a sellers freedom to charge as they want, but you also allow consumers to make more optimal choices.

I am submitting this comment as an ordinary consumer. I am not affiliated with any company, trade group, or organization.I believe personalized pricing based on data surveillance is wrong, and that allowing it to continue unchecked puts us on a very slippery slope. But the part that alarms me most is how few people know it is happening at all.
Before writing this, I asked my husband, my family, and my friends. Not one of them knew this was going on, or that it was even possible. Every one of them assumed that the price on a website is simply the price, the same number anyone else would see. That assumption is so basic that most people have never thought to question it.
What prompted me to look into this was a video I came across in which three people in the same city pulled up the same item on target.com — a can of Spam — and were each shown a different price. The same group repeated the test on Uber, scheduling the same pickup and drop-off for the same date and time, and got wildly different fares. They tried it again booking a hotel, with the same result. Nowhere on any of those sites was there a word telling them the price they were seeing had been shaped by their own data.
That omission is the whole problem. If a retailer told me plainly that my price was personalized, I would act differently. I would comparison shop, check another device, clear my browser, look at a competitor — I would not simply accept the first number I was given. Without that disclosure, I do not know there is anything to push back against. Silence is what makes the practice work, and silence is what makes it unfair.
This hands corporations an enormous advantage over the average consumer, who has no way to detect it and no idea to look for it. And I have to ask where it ends. If companies can use these methods unrestricted and under the radar, what stops the inputs from expanding? Race. Income. Occupation. Marital status. Number of children. Age. Gender. Spending habits. These are exactly the characteristics we have decided, as a country, that people should not be treated differently on. If consumers are protected from discrimination in the workplace, why should they not have comparable protection at the point of sale?
I want to note the scale of public reaction here, because I think it speaks to the deception issue directly. Beyond my own informal polling of the people around me, the video I referenced — posted on tiktok by the account @christheproducer21 — has drawn over 16,600 comments. The overwhelming response is shock and outrage, and, more tellingly, complete unawareness that this was ever happening. When a practice can operate for years without the public having any idea of it, that is strong evidence that it defies reasonable consumer expectations.
My position is that this should not be happening at all. If you and your neighbors live in the same city and shop at the same store, the price should be the same across the board.
If the Commission concludes it cannot prohibit the practice outright, then at an absolute minimum the disclosure requirement must be real:
 1. It must appear where the price appears — on the product page, at the moment I see the number — not buried in a privacy policy or terms of service that no one reads.
 2. It must state clearly that the price is personalized, identify the categories of personal data used, and explain how that data affected the price I am being shown.
 3. It must be specific enough that an ordinary person can act on it, because a disclosure that does not let me change my behavior is not a disclosure at all.
Most people today are juggling more than enough already. They should not also have to worry that the store is quietly sizing them up. I urge the Commission to adopt the strongest possible reading of its Section 5 authority here and to enforce it aggressively.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Please ban personalized pricing. This leads to discriminatory and predatory behaviors from corporations. The people of the USA deserve transparency, equal opportunity, privacy, and freedom. Please also ban mass data collection and surveillance that is used in the personalized pricing schemes and in general.

Dear FTC Staff,

So-called “personalized pricing”, otherwise known as surveillance pricing, must be completely outlawed. I’m surprised we even have to comment about such a thing. In your heart you know it’s wrong.

Sincerely,
Thomas A. Ceresini

why should a company be allowed to charge two people different price for the same object. What metric will they use, my sex, my race, the clothes I wear? This seams to have the potential to be very discriminatory.

- That the price is personalized rather than broadly available.
- The principal data categories and factors used to set it.
- Whether the consumer is receiving a discount or paying more than a generally available reference price.
- The dollar amount—or, at minimum, the percentage—by which the personalized price differs from the standard price.

To the Commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission:

I write to urge the Commission, in the strongest possible terms, to pursue rulemaking and enforcement action that would make personalized pricing — the practice of charging different consumers different prices for identical goods or services based on data collected about them individually — unlawful in the United States. This practice is not a neutral pricing innovation. It is a systematic exploitation of the information asymmetry between firms and consumers, and it should be treated as an unfair and deceptive practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

1. Personalized pricing inverts the basic premise of a competitive market

Markets are supposed to work because consumers can compare prices and firms compete for their business on a level playing field. Personalized pricing destroys that premise. When a firm knows a consumer's income bracket, browsing history, device type, location, purchase urgency, or even how long they hesitated before clicking "buy," it can calculate the maximum that specific individual will pay — and charge exactly that. This is not price discovery. It is the elimination of the consumer's ability to shop, compare, or negotiate in any meaningful sense, because the "market price" no longer exists as a stable, comparable reference point. Every consumer effectively faces a market of one, priced against them by an entity with vastly superior information.

2. It is built on nonconsensual surveillance

Personalized pricing depends on extensive behavioral profiling: tracking cookies, device fingerprinting, purchase history, geolocation, and inferred demographic and psychographic data, frequently obtained and combined without consumers' meaningful knowledge or consent. Consumers do not expect — and did not agree — to have their willingness to pay algorithmically estimated and monetized. The Commission has long treated covert data practices that harm consumers as a core area of concern; personalized pricing should be recognized as one of the clearest cases where covert data collection translates directly into concrete financial injury.

3. It disproportionately harms the consumers least able to detect or resist it

Evidence gathered by researchers and journalists has repeatedly shown that algorithmic pricing systems can charge more to consumers in lower-income ZIP codes, to consumers using older or lower-cost devices, to consumers with less time to shop around, and to consumers in areas with fewer retail alternatives. Far from personalization delivering better deals to price-sensitive shoppers, the incentive structure runs the other way: the algorithm's entire purpose is to find the highest price each individual will tolerate. This is regressive by design and falls hardest on people with the least market power.

4. Existing legal frameworks are inadequate to the scale of the practice

The Robinson-Patman Act addresses price discrimination between business purchasers, not consumer-facing algorithmic pricing. State-level unfair-practices statutes are inconsistent and rarely equipped to address opaque, real-time algorithmic pricing at scale. Only the FTC, exercising its Section 5 authority over unfair and deceptive acts and practices, has both the jurisdiction and the technical capacity to address this as a nationwide practice. The Commission's own 2024 study on surveillance pricing confirmed that firms are actively developing and deploying these tools; the time for a study-only posture has passed.

5. Recommended Commission action

I urge the Commission to:

Issue a rule under Section 5 categorically prohibiting the use of individually-targeted, non-transparent price variation based on personal data unrelated to the actual cost of providing the good or service.
Require disclosure at minimum, as an interim step, mandating that any price shown to a consumer that differs from a general list price due to personalized factors be conspicuously labeled as such, with an explanation of what data was used.
Ban the use of protected or proxy-protected characteristics (race, income proxies, disability status, age, ZIP code as a proxy for demographic composition) in any pricing algorithm, full stop.
Compel algorithmic transparency and audit rights, requiring firms deploying dynamic or personalized pricing systems to make them available for independent, ongoing regulatory audit.
Impose meaningful penalties, including disgorgement of profits attributable to personalized pricing, sufficient to remove the financial incentive for noncompliance.

Personalized pricing is not a minor pricing technique — it is a fundamental threat to the basic bargain of a fair marketplace: that price is public, comparable, and not secretly calibrated to extract the maximum a given individual can be made to pay. I urge the Commission to act decisively and treat this as the urgent consumer protection issue it is.

Re: FTC-2026-1057 — Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing

I strongly oppose personalized pricing based on consumer data and support the FTC’s efforts to investigate and restrict this practice.

Consumers reasonably expect that a listed price is determined by the product, service, and ordinary market conditions—not by a hidden calculation of how much a particular person might be willing or forced to pay. Using browsing history, location, purchase history, household composition, medical circumstances, financial information, or other personal data to charge different consumers different prices is fundamentally deceptive when it occurs without their knowledge.

Personalized pricing also undermines meaningful comparison shopping. A competitive market depends on consumers being able to compare the same offers. If each consumer sees a different price based on information collected about that person, there is no longer a reliable market price to compare. Consumers cannot make informed choices when they do not know whether the displayed price reflects the value of the product or an algorithm’s estimate of their vulnerability, urgency, or ability to pay.

I am particularly concerned about pricing based on sensitive circumstances. A person should never pay more because data suggest that the person is experiencing a medical emergency, traveling for a funeral, caring for children, recently experienced a crime, lacks transportation, or has few practical alternatives. Disclosing that such exploitation is occurring would not necessarily make it fair. Certain uses of personal data should be considered unfair even when disclosed because the consumer may have no reasonable way to avoid the harm.

Personalized pricing also creates serious privacy and discrimination concerns. Algorithms may use seemingly neutral information as a proxy for income, disability, race, age, family status, religion, health, or geographic location. Consumers may never know what information was used, whether it was accurate, or how to correct it. Businesses should not be permitted to avoid responsibility by outsourcing these decisions to data brokers, software vendors, or pricing algorithms.

As a small-business owner and healthcare professional, I recognize that not every price difference is improper. Prices may legitimately vary because of differences in products, services, costs, insurance contracts, publicly disclosed discounts, geographic markets, or changing supply and demand. Those ordinary and explainable differences are distinct from secretly charging an individual more because data suggest that the person will tolerate a higher price.

I urge the FTC to finalize and strengthen its proposed policy by:

1. Requiring clear, prominent disclosure whenever personal data influence a consumer’s price.
2. Requiring disclosure of the specific basis and categories of data used—not vague phrases such as “special price” or “personalized offer.”
3. Giving consumers access to a non-personalized price and a meaningful opportunity to opt out.
4. Holding businesses responsible for pricing decisions made by their vendors and automated systems.
5. Treating the use of health information, emergencies, personal hardship, or other vulnerabilities to increase prices as presumptively unfair.
6. Requiring a practical process for consumers to identify and correct inaccurate information.
7. Preserving the FTC’s ability to find that certain personalized-pricing practices are unfair even when technically disclosed.

A person’s private information should not become a tool for extracting the highest price that person can be pressured into paying. Americans deserve transparent prices, genuine competition, and confidence that personal data will not be used against them. I encourage the Commission to adopt the strongest protections available under its existing authority and to recommend additional congressional action if further authority is needed.

I have been a practitioner and teacher of antitrust law from my graduation from 
Harvard Law School in 1967 to my recent retirement as a law firm partner 
specializing in the antitrust aspects of mergers and acquisitions. A highlight of my 
career was my stint from 1977-79 as an Assistant Director for General Litigation in 
the FTC's Bureau of Competition. 

The FTC that I knew, respected (and, indeed, loved) during my time there and for 
many years thereafter was an essentially nonpartisan institution manned to a great 
extent by career employees of unquestionable dedication and devotion to serving 
the competition mission with fairness and impartiality, and overseen by senior 
managers and commissioners who largely shared that public service mindset. 

One of the mainstays of FTC practice was the existence of the administrative law 
judge who managed the administrative hearing process. The ALJ's actions were, of 
course, subject to Commission review and the ultimate Commission decision, but the 
ALJ's status -- at one remove from the fray, and typically with the respect earned 
through years of experience at this important work -- provided both the appearance 
and reality of impartiality. And what can be more important than that in an 
adjudicatory setting?

While the shortness of time allowed by the 30-day comment period allows only 
these brief preliminary comments, I do want to make the following points:

(1) 30 days is too brief for comments on a proposal that would make such drastic 
changes in the administrative process at the FTC. Why such a rush? Why foreclose 
the opportunity for considered comments by antitrust scholars, practitioners and 
organizations, and for reasoned consideration by the Commission of these 
comments? In this election year, the truncated timing of the comment period 
suggests a rush to resolve this matter before a change of administrations and in the 
membership of the Commission. Hopefully, this result was unintended, but 
nonetheless the perception of an unseemly rush to change the long-established 
rules does not serve the Commission well.

(2) A rigid time frame for the commencement of an administrative hearing is a one-
size-fits-all solution for diverse situations that can better be managed by an 
experienced ALJ who can impartially assess the needs of a particular case, including 
the amount of time necessary for the respondent to have a fair opportunity to 
prepare its defense. This is exactly the kind of nitty gritty hands-on function that 
ALJs perform so well. 

(3) Continuing to entrust the ALJs with responsibility for pretrial motions keeps 
responsibility for case management centered in the hands of the FTC official with the 
closest and best view of the case in the pretrial and administrative trial phases, as 
well as some independence from the initial decision to vote out a complaint. Absent 
a factual showing of disabling deficiencies in this process, which has served the 
Commission and litigants well for many years, this long-established practice should 
not be abandoned. The appearance of the Commission reaching to micromanage 
and control pretrial proceedings marks a profound change in the administrative 
process. As a young antitrust lawyer, I recall marveling at the strangeness of the 
Commission voting out a complaint as prosecutors and then putting on judge's hats 
and sitting in judgment on the case that they initiated: it is useful for all of us to 
continue to appreciate what a curious system this is. I came to think of the time that 
the case was in the hands of the ALJ as a sort of cooling off period, where others 
could work up the facts and assess the theories and bring considered work product 
back for the consideration of the Commission in its adjudicatory role: why mandate 
Commissioner intrusion into this phase too? 

Respectfully submitted,
Linda Blumkin

The Federal Trade Commission's (the FTC) enforcement action and proposed 
consent agreement with We Give Loans, Inc. (a.k.a. the Perpetrators), FTC File 
No.: 072-3205, is deplorable. What we have here is an advertiser of consumer 
loan products who willfully, knowingly and negligently failed in each and every way 
to disclose important loan terms in their consumer loan advertising as is required 
by the federal Truth-in-Lending Act (TILA) and Federal Reserve Board Regulation 
Z, the TILAs implementing federal regulations. 

However, in response to We Give Loans, Inc.'s innumerable violations of federal 
consumer protection advertising laws, the FTC proposes a consent order that 
merely requires these Perpetrators to comply in the future with all of the consumer 
lending advertising laws that they failed to comply with in the past. Why the hell 
is the FTC letting them off with less than a slap on the wrist. Obviously, all the 
Perp's will have to do is set up a new corporation that is entirely unrelated to We 
Give Loans, Inc. and run their business through it and entirely outside the watchful 
eyes of the FTC. They'll slow down the operations of We Give Loans, Inc. to the 
point that corporation is listed as active and in good standing by the Delaware 
Secretary of State. Eventually, after 5 years have passed, they'll just dissolve 
We Give Loans, Inc. and disburse any remaining assets to the principals. There 
will be no need to notify the FTC of the new corporation they've been running their 
business through because it's unrelated to the We Give Loans, Inc.

I'll bet the We Give Loans, Inc. folks were about the happiest deceptive advertisers 
in the country once they read through your proposed consent order and found out 
they were going to be required to do what they should have been doing all along. 
Unfortunately, whenever enforcement actions are issued against violators of 
consumer protection laws that are barely even a slap on the wrist, the public 
begins to wonder why the government enforcement agency went so easy on the 
consumer protection violators. With human nature as it is, the public begins to 
wonder if the reason for violators got off so easy is because of certain incentives 
that may have been offered to, and accepted by, agency personnel. While it's 
distressing to even imagine this could happen, we know that it has been 
somewhat common in certain other enforcement agencies. We are prayerful that 
this is not what has happened in this case.

Perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the FTC's enforcement of consumer 
advertising regulations against We Give Loans, Inc. is the absence of any civil 
money penalties. Why the hell the FTC doesn't hit the Perpetrators up for 
somewhere between $100,000 and $1,000,000 dollars for their deceptive 
consumer loan advertising is a question we must all ask over and over. By giving 
the Perp's a slap on the wrist instead of busting them on their ass for deceiving 
consumers, the FTC is inviting others to follow in the footsteps of We Give Loans, 
Inc. In fact, the risk of these deceptive advertisers being caught in the first place 
is very low, and if they are caught, chances are high that they'll just get a slap on 
the wrist and no civil money penalties. Add all this together and these consumer 
loan advertisers end up with a Risk Assessment that tells them they're nuts to 
even bother with adding required consumer disclosures to their advertising.

Way to drop the ball FTC. Given the fact that the enforcement actions you issue 
are nothing more than a fractional fraction of all the consumer protection violations 
that go unchallenged, uninvestigated and unenforced day in and day out, the FTC 
should make the most of each opportunity it has to enforce the law to show all the 
baddies that the last thing they'll ever want is to get caught violating consumer 
protection laws. As it is now though, there's little if any fear that any 
consequences will be suffered by the baddies.

(2) Are any specific provisions of the Leather Guides no longer necessary?

The Leather Guides do overlap, but however, to my knowledge do not conflict with Federal laws. I am a manager in a high-tech, US-based, secure computer design and manufacturing firm. We have run into significant problems from certain component vendors that overlap with right to repair legislation. Specifically, certain vendors require all firmware components to be signed with their vendor key in order for the firmware to execute. This severely impairs the repair capability of their devices, increases e-waste when the vendor is unwilling to fix known bugs in their firmware (recommending for instance to buy a newer or more expensive device and discard the old one) and also severely limits innovation in fields that the vendor has not considered.

When the vendor is the only manufacturer creating a specific class of computing peripheral, this has the effect of not only stifling repair of entire classes of devices, but also encouraging foreign (usually Asian) companies to innovate where US citizens and corporations are locked out by vendor decisions.

Any right to repair guidelines in today's high tech, firmware-driven world must address the issue of vendor cryptographic signatures being required to replace existing malfunctioning firmware on hardware devices. Ideally this would take the form of an alternate operating mode being required that does not check the firmware signature, but also indicates the device is operating outside of the vendor controlled mode. This would allow e.g. DRM systems to function on the vendor firmware, but still allow owner repair / replacement of firmware with deactivation of the DRM systems (i.e. inability to decrypt protected content using unsigned firmware, but the ability to repair the rest of the device functionality).

We have already seen significant damage in the overall economy, ranging from impacts caused by the signed Intel ME/ AMD PSP along with, for example, NVIDIA's cryptographic signing forcing continual replacement of otherwise functional cards. This requirement to replace and discard is usually due to firmware or firmware-enforced driver bugs that NVIDIA is unwilling to fix for commercial reasons.

Please take action and put a stop to this, allow American companies to innovate again, reduce our e-waste, and restore the right to repair complex firmware-driven systems.

9) The legal violations of the Franchise Agreement, by both Alphabet and the City of New York, through the integration of video, audio, and photographic recording and sensing capabilities into the LinkNYC Wi-Fi units, as well as the inclusion of a Web browser.

Increasingly apartment communities are providing building-wide networks for tenants to use. My own apartment complex requires the use of this network to use sort-of wired broadband at all, which provides excellent Internet bandwidth but impairs the performance of or often outright breaks local networking. That is, a failure in Charter's equipment can prevent and has prevented my laptop from talking to my desktop, and I'm not legally allowed to fix it by connecting to the Internet through my own network--the best I can do is connect up to two devices through an Ethernet switch. Charter won't sell normal service to me without permission from the property owners, which I haven't gotten despite complaining for more than six months; and their contract somehow forbids me from buying service from AT&T.

Charter's network doesn't support inbound connections at all, so if you want to host a Minecraft game for remote friends you're out of luck.

Charter's network uses a weak password users cannot change for initial sign-on, then uses easily spoofed MAC addresses to authenticate connections to the network from that device. A moderately over-achieving 14-year-old can commit online crimes and make it look like they're happening from my apartment, and there's nothing I can do to stop them without disconnecting all of my devices from the connection permanently. And that only works if they can't guess the password to just authorize their own device. Routing local traffic through the ISP's equipment also raises privacy and civil rights concerns--is my LAN traffic now also subject to wiretap orders? Is Charter gathering information about the types of computers and local network services I use? Does Charter have the technical ability to attempt to connect to those services which ought to be exposed only to members of my household?

As ISPs push these "community WiFi" solutions on additional apartment communities, problems like these will plague more and more people in America's largest population centers and will become harder and harder for consumers who cannot or should not buy their own real estate to escape.

These agreements to allow Charter's or any other ISP's own managed network to be the exclusive sort-of-wired broadband for a property are an end-run around FCC regulations requiring cable subscribers be allowed to attach their own equipment to the cable network, they inextricably tie Internet providers to apartments, they severely limit what consumers can do with their own local networks, and this non-legal-expert isn't even sure how this is allowed under the Sherman Antitrust Act. 

Not only do I think these agreements should be outright banned, but services like this raise questions about how we define the term 'Internet access.' Users forced to use these connections cannot be full Internet participants and limited service like this should not be sold as equivalent to or better than residential wired broadband.

The Federal Trade Commission and other regulatory bodies have not yet provided to the public a clear definition for reasonable cybersecurity management.

In April 2018 Center for Internet Security (CIS) published their method for assessing cybersecurity risk to determine whether safeguards are reasonable and appropriate as regulators, litigators, and information security practitioners use the terms. CIS Risk Assessment Method (CIS RAM) describes a process for evaluating cybersecurity risk to determine whether an organizations controls environment:
1. Creates the foreseeability of harm that would be acceptable to the organization and to others.
2. Presents a reasonable burden on the organization.

CIS RAM based on the Duty of Care Risk Analysis (DoCRA) Standard provides a model for analyzing risks that supports:
1. Long-established standards for regulatory oversight using cost-benefit analysis (viz. Executive Order 12866, 1993).
2. Common regulatory requirements for using risk analysis to establish reasonableness of security controls (e.g. HIPAA Security Rule, GLBA Safeguards Rule, 23 NYCRR Part 500, Massachusetts 201 CMR 17.00, etc.).
3. Multifactor balancing tests used by courts to determine the reasonableness or negligence of defendants.
4. Information security standards for assessing information security risk (NIST Special Publications 800-30, ISO 27005, RISK IT).

Additionally, the model in CIS RAM supports FTCs consistent guidance to the public and to breached organizations for using risk management as a basis for comprehensive security and risk management programs (even despite the benefit of security certifications, e.g. Statement of the Federal Trade Commission. FTC v. LifeLock, December 17, 2015).

Because CIS RAM and DoCRA are simply practical models for long-established standards and requirements, FTC and other regulators who refer to these methods will be consistent with well-established enforcement practices.
1. Oversight actions that evaluate whether an organization uses reasonable controls may include review of the organizations risk assessments. Because risk assessments are common requirements to determine the reasonableness of safeguards, these documents should be in-hand as a record of the organizations evaluation of reasonableness. Lack of risk assessments that demonstrate the balance of safeguards against the likelihood and impact of foreseeable threats could clearly constitute an organizations lack of managing reasonable and appropriate controls.
2. Consent orders and injunctive relief that require organizations to improve their security programs can be based on an evaluation of their controls environment, and a proposal for controls that evaluate as reasonable and appropriate as described in the CIS RAM and DoCRA documents.

CIS (Center for Internet Security, Inc.) is a forward-thinking, non-profit entity that harnesses the power of a global IT community to safeguard private and public organizations against cyber threats. Our CIS Controls and CIS Benchmarks are the global standard and recognized best practices for securing IT systems and data against the most pervasive attacks. These proven guidelines are continuously refined and verified by a volunteer, global community of experienced IT professionals. CIS is home to the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MSISAC), the go-to resource for cyber threat prevention, protection, response, and recovery for U.S. State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial government entities. The Federal Trade Commission is doing a great job in the area of information security and privacy. I strongly support your work, and the approach you have taken. I agree with the FTC's focus on "reasonable and appropriate" security and privacy, as that relates to a specific organization. Information security and privacy must be tailored to the organization in question and thus it is often at odds with the rigidity, definitive character, and slow pace of change found in the realm of laws and regulations. If the FTC should further elaborate on what exactly it means by "reasonable and appropriate" and how it goes about determining this conceptual line. That specificity would help organizations justify, and later install and operate the proper information security and privacy controls.

There is one conceptual shift which I urge the FTC to adopt and that has to do with the parties that can actually make changes so that "reasonable and appropriate" information security and privacy can be manifested. Many of the consent decrees which the FTC has reached appear to assume that a user organization is fully responsible for, and the party in a position to manifest, a "reasonable and appropriate" level of information security and privacy. In many cases this assumption does not match up with reality. With the exception of the largest and most successful firms, user organizations must use the technological tools that they can buy, rent, lease, or subscribe to. Their "bag of tricks" is thus defined by the marketplace. The vast majority of user organizations are not in a position to invent new tools, technologies, and/or approaches. They can only use what is on the marketplace, and attempt to cobble together some combination of those market offerings, and then hold all that together with some internal infrastructure, like training, policies, and procedures. The offerings in this "bag of tricks" are very limited, and often the firms that make these offerings available do not place a high value on security or privacy. 

The vendors providing the tools for information security and privacy need to be held liable and culpable for problems related to the information security and privacy impacts of their tools much more often than they are now. To expect things to change because the FTC pursues user organizations rather than the vendors, is assigning blame, liability, and culpability to the organizations that do not have the power, knowledge, or expertise necessary to make changes to the tools used to establish and maintain "reasonable and appropriate" information security and privacy. A much greater focus of the FTC's enforcement activity should thus be on the information systems and network vendors, and whether they have provided the tools which can in fact establish a "reasonable and appropriate" level of information security and privacy. 

Furthermore, assigning civil liability and criminal culpability to the vendors of tools will help to motivate them to upgrade their tools, so that the user organizations can then, as a result, operate with "reasonable and appropriate" information security and privacy. The burden placed on user organizations these days, for instance to stay on top of all the patches issued by vendors of software, is excessive and inappropriate, and it entails a transfer of legal responsibility for information security and privacy from the vendors to the user organizations. The responsibility should, in large measure, be shifted back to the vendors, because the vendors are often the only parties which are in a position to do anything about the types of tools available, and the embedded security and privacy found in those same tools. 

- Charles Cresson Wood, Esq., MBA, MSE, CISA, CISSP, CISM, CGEIT
Independent Information Security and Privacy Consultant with 40 years of experience in the field

The FTC and Congress must coordinate efforts to address data-driven discrimination. Right now we have weak, piecemeal regulations and weak enforcement. The U.S. must create and enforce regulations similar to the EU's GDPR. Loot boxes function as mini slot machines that allow individuals to use real money to gamble for digital rewards. While some items are purely cosmetic (which could be sold for a flat price anyways), some items make a character more powerful, the game easier, or open up new options in the game with creates a, "Pay to win," experience. As a gamer let me tell you, loot boxes have gotten out of control in the last 3-5 years. The gaming community has tried for years and years to get them under control. We have repeatedly warned developers and publishers that if they do not self-regulate and learn to control their runaway greed in regards to loot boxes that the government will eventually have to step in and regulate loot boxes for them. They chose not listen and so here we are. 

When possible I like to avoid needless government regulation. I believe the government should only step in when two conditions are met. First, when people or corporations have shown they lack the ability to, or are unwilling to, self-regulate. Second, when there is a genuine and growing harm done by not regulating. The first is unquestionably true. Gaming companies have time and time again expanded loot box systems, made them more predatory, and even done what they could to specifically target children with them. They have done everything possible to make them more profitable without even considering the affect these things are having on anyone, including children. I believe the second condition has been met as well. Game companies have spent years analyzing data on how people interact with loot boxes. They are designed to be addictive and it is having a very negative affect on children. Children are simply not mentally equipped with the necessary tools to avoid targeted addiction at this level. In closing I just want to say that I'm glad that someone is finally willing to step in and look into this growing problem. If a game allows items obtained from loot boxes to be traded to other players in any way, then those loot boxes should fall under the standard regulations applied to other forms of gambling, as players are paying actual money for loot boxes, and have the potential to make actual money back from them (whether sale of items is facilitated by the game publishers or must be done external to any systems set up by the publishers). This includes insuring that no minors can possibly purchase loot boxes.
If a game does not allow items obtained from loot boxes to be traded to other players, then they should still be regulated in some ways, but not necessarily in exactly the same way as other forms of gambling. At a minimum it should be required that the odds of obtaining any specific item from a loot box should be clearly stated and/or a system should be set up to allow players to allow players to purchase any specific item after a certain number of loot boxes have been opened (for example: a system whereby items obtained can be traded in for an in-game currency that can be used to buy any loot box items for set prices, with a minimum guaranteed amount of the in-game currency that can be obtained from each loot box). The key is that players need to be able to make an informed decision when there's a specific item from a loot box that they hope to get. A player should be able to look at a specific item and say "based on those odds I'm likely to have to spend X amount to get that item" or "based on the amount of in-game currency I can get from each loot box I'll be able to buy that item after buying no more than X loot boxes", and it should be easy for players to come to such conclusions. Anything less than that is simply unethical, as it relies on player ignorance and predatory psychology to obfuscate the actual amount that players are likely to have to spend while encouraging players to sink more and more money into gambling (the psychological effect of the sunk cost fallacy is a major factor) in the hopes that this time they'll be lucky. Some protections for minors are likely appropriate for these types of loot boxes as well, and experts on child psychology and the psychology of gambling addicts should be consulted to determine how extensive these protections should be.

There is currently an unreasonably high prevalence of all types of repair restrictions in the United States. Economic stagnation, reduced productivity, and consumer financial duress are the predictable results from all types of repair restrictions. Manufacturers repair restrictions impact small and local businesses the hardestleading to greatly reduced market competitiveness and higher concentrations of market power in larger corporate manufacturers.

 The market distortions created by manufacturers repair restrictions have caused increased prices for repairing goods to often-times unjustifiably exceed the cost of purchasing a replacement product, thus generating excessive waste from the disposal of otherwise reusable components. The accessibility and timeliness of repairs, and the quality of repairs, are further degraded by manufacturers repair restrictions, as many limitationsboth financially and logisticallymay unduly burden and impair consumers from accessing a manufacturers authorized repair service.

 Independent repair shops and consumers ability to repair warrantied products are effectively marginalized into near impossibility by manufacturers repair restrictions, unless the owner of the device in question is willing to void the warranty or to risk other forms of retaliation by manufacturersin particular, the use of so-called Digital Rights Management (DRM) allows manufacturers to legally accuse independent repair shops and consumers of violating the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA). 

 Consumers and independent repair shops risk possible legal retaliatory actions under the DMCA simply for trying to repair a device, if repairs for certain devices unjustly require circumventing DRM restrictions embedded within certain devices by manufacturersand manufacturers often embed DRM in devices solely for the purpose of unjustly monopolizing the repair process.
 
 Manufacturers have no legitimate justifications for repair restrictions, or for using DRM to monopolize the repair process. The only basis for such supposed justifications is to further corporate profit by anti-competitive means, including furthering the sale of services, extended warranties, or entirely new replacement devices by manufacturersand thus generating unnecessary waste, by unduly shortening product life cycles through artificial repair restrictions.

 The are no legitimate risks to the general welfare or public posed by repairs made by consumers or independent repair shops, but instead only benefitsbenefits such as increasing competition in the broader marketplace, encouraging new market participants to enter the repair business, decreasing monopolistic tendencies, increasing market productivity, and further benefiting the environment by reducing waste from the unnecessary early replacement of devices. 

 Any liability faced by manufacturers when consumers, or independent repair workers, are injured while repairing a product (or injured after using or coming into contact with a product that has been repaired improperly), can be mitigated and indemnified by an act of Congress or by rule-making at the regulatory level, and is therefore not a legitimate business concern, but is rather an anti-competitive ruse used by manufacturers to attempt to maintain market dominance and to crowd-out competitors.

 Further, consumersor, more properly, the property owners of the chattel in question for repairmost often do not understand the existence of repair restrictions, and the effects lead to potentially unjustifiable legal liability for consumers after simply trying to repair their own personal possessionsespecially in the presence of DRM. 

 Consumers also do not understand the potential repercussions if they face prosecution under the DMCA for repairing their own personal devices that have DRM embedded into their property (as the device to be repaired is the chattel of the property owner, and so the consumer is also a property owner in this regard).

 Finally, repairs made by consumers, or by independent repair shops, should be considered to be covered by the 9th Amendments protection of unenumerated rights, as manufacturers repair restrictions deny or disparage [rights] retained by the people to repair their own personal possessions. The right to repair personal possessions (or chattel) surely existed both before and after the ratification of the Constitution, and should therefore properly be viewed within the light of the 9th Amendmentespecially, when considering that the right to repair such goods and chattels has only become encumbered within recent times by the relatively new anti-competitive practice of repair restrictions.

Franchise Rule Regulatory Review, 16 CFR part 436, Matter No. R511003
Response to Question 1 "Is there a continuing need for the Rule? Why or why not?"

I think there is a continue need of this rule.

On one hand, the rule requires the franchisors to provide specific and detailed information about the franchise business for the prospective franchisees, which is helpful for the legality of the contract. Prospective franchisees might better know about the franchise business before entering into the contract and thus avoid a lot of loss that might be caused by the "fradulent franchise business" contract. In addition, if there is any dispute between the two parties, the detailed disclosure might be a powerful and informative lawful evidence in the potential lawsuit.

On the other hand, the rule should be continued because franchisors can also benefit from this rule. Intangible assets such as brand name will be involved in the franchisor-franchisee relationships and sometimes the intangibles might be diminished if they are not fully stated and specified in the Franchise Disclosure Document . If these intangibles are clearly stated in the document, both parties can see their rights and obligations and deal with them properly.

The last reason would be that fully disclosed info is good for being audit, and audited info is more reliable.

Franchise Rule Regulatory Review, 16 CFR part 436, Matter No. R511003

There is a continuing need for the Rule because the whole reason behind this Rule was to protect the interests and assets of prospective franchise purchasers. Buying a franchise costs a lot of money, and they will be met with consequences that will make lasting impact, so having such an extensive disclosure process is only beneficial to help prospective franchise purchasers reduce information asymmetry and enable them to make a more informed disclosure. The Rule was recently amended to reduce the inconsistency in reporting between states, but there was a concern that this might also compromise on the amount of information that will be provided to prospective franchise purchasers. In my opinion, the amount of historical and financial information is very necessary, but not enough. Purchasing a franchise goes beyond just the historical and financial data there are other factors that are critical in considering the purchase of a franchise, such as reputation, especially on media. These franchises depend so much on reputation and that is beyond what historical and financial numbers can portray; therefore, there should be an analysis regarding the success of its marketing efforts be it on social media, traditional media, or non-traditional media, and include the franchises main issues in terms of brand image, and what they are aiming to achieve. With franchises, it is often a challenge to keep their image consistent since they are owned by different people, but brand image affects the success of the business so much that I think it is necessary to take into account one of the most essential factors needed to build trust with future customers.

I have some different ideas about the exceptions of proposed section 314.6. It talked about exempting some small institutions from several requirements, and the reason for this exemption is that some requirements are too expensive for small institutions to afford. I agree with the idea that this exemption can help institutions which have relatively small amounts of customer information reduce their financial burden, but I think these subsections are also very important for protecting customers' information, so it would be more helpful if we can keep them. Thus, from my perspective, these paragraphs should not be directly exempted. On the contrary, it would be better if the rule makes these exemptions optional for small institutions, which means they can choose whether they will follow these subsections or not according to their own financial situation. The FTC should address the growing issue of hospital prices and their impact
on mergers with independent physicians, competition and consumer pricing.
The FTC should study the impact hospital mergers have on "quality" through a framework of measurable standard outcomes.

As of writing this, I am close to obtaining an Associate's Degree as a Paralegal. Yet despite adulthood, I am a gamer; I play video games for fun and have since my days as a child. I have seen the video game industry grow and change in a vast amount of ways. Today, the pressing issue with the industry is the matter of Microtransactions, game content that a player would purchase with real money in a video game that they may have already spent money to purchase, but rather specifically on Loot Boxes. For those who are not aware, Loot Boxes are a form of video game Microtransaction, which players open to reveal a random selection of in-game items. Make no mistake with this; Loot Boxes are a form of gambling, and so are in dire need for regulation, if not being banned from video games.

Why are Loot Boxes gambling?

Presently, gambling is defined to have three components: Consideration, risk (or chance), and a prize. Loot Boxes, as they stand, have all three of these components. First, Loot Boxes are typically obtained through the purchase of real-world money, which is the Consideration. Second, the risk or the chance. This is perhaps the most ambiguous, since Risk is often interpreted to the likelihood of loss. I would argue that the focus should be more on the fact that the outcome itself is uncertain. The player has absolutely no input on the outcome, or in this case, the player has no control over what prizes are in a Loot Box. Another way to see Risk in Loot Boxes is the possibility of the player not receiving their desired loot; often times, the desired loot are the most rarest, which leads to Prize. Third, Prizes are obviously present in Loot Boxes. They come in the form of in-game items that players then may use, which these uses ranging from gaining a competitive advantage or simply for cosmetic purposes. These are the items that players seek, and often times these Loot Boxes are the only means for players to obtain them. These Prizes often have real-world value; an example of this is in the online tactical game Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, where players may open up crates for weapon "skins" which players may sell on the online Steam marketplace. Even if players cannot trade these in-game items, these in-game items still retain real-world value, through the fact that it has costed money to purchase the Loot Box they came in. With all this in consideration, it is safe to say that Loot Boxes are a form of gambling, simply in a different form targeting a different demographic. 

Then, there are the feelings elicited. As I said before, I am in the process of earning an Associate's degree. I am currently old enough to drink alcohol and gamble at a casino. And I do gamble at casinos. Whenever I engage with these Loot Boxes, it feels as though I am in front a slot machine, waiting for each wheel to stop spinning, eager to see trails of lights illuminate across while chirping away with what winnings I obtained, if I won any to begin with. By deliberate design, Loot Boxes invoke these psychological stimuli that are the equivalent to slot machines. 

These feelings of being "lulled" into Loot Boxes in the same way a slot machine does is not idle speculation. Academic journals have been published with their findings being consistent on the idea that Loot Boxes invoke those feelings that are equal to when one gambles. 

An academic paper authored by David Zendle of York St. John University and Paul Cairns of the University of York (Article has been attached at Attachment1_Academic Report 1.pdf; also a minor correction attached as Attachment1_Academic Report 1_Correction.pdf), in a study of over 11,000 participants, that strong relationships between Problem Gambling and Loot Boxes appear to exist, a relationship that they have noted was stronger than the relationships between Problem Gambling and depression and was comparable with the relationship between Problem Gambling and alcohol dependence. 

Another paper published by Daniel L. King and Paul H. Delfabbro of the University of Adelaide (Attached as Attachment2_Academic Report 2.pdf) warns against Loot Boxes and stresses that meticulous research should be done to study the long-term effects of Loot Boxes and the consequences found in various other money-making schemes found in the video game industry.

So to go back to the topic at hand, why should Loot Boxes be regulated?

The simple fact is that a large demographic of gamers are kids and teenagers. These age groups are far too young to drink or even gamble, thus are vulnerable, yet they are continuously targeted by an industry who hope to exploit them for quick cash and treating them as potential addicts. This is unacceptable. We should not allow them to be targeted the same way tobacco companies once did.

For the well-being of kids and teenagers, and the integrity of video games, Loot Boxes must be regulated as gambling, if not banned from video games that are rated and targeting kids and teenagers.

Dear Acting Secretary Tabor:
I write to submit these comments in response to the Federal Trade Commission's ("FTC") request for public comment on its Trade Regulation Rule entitled "Disclosure Requirements and Prohibitions Concerning Franchising" (the "Rule"), published in the Federal Register on March 13, 2019 (84 Fed. Reg. 9051). 
Under the franchise business model, every franchise brand involves both a franchisor and a network of franchisees. Franchisees are individual business owners who have secured a license from the franchisor, or parent brand, to own and operate a business using that brands trade name. Such arrangements typically require the franchisor to provide support for the franchisees, including standards regarding quality and uniformity, as well as brand-related investments such as national advertising, but the business owner is responsible for his or her own business, particularly hiring, firing, scheduling, and maintenance. The franchise business model allows many small business owners to be in business for themselves, but not by themselves. This system is based on the principle that every franchisee, owns and operates his or her own business and are responsible for their own decisions. Franchisees also retain their own business-related profits.
Nationwide, franchising accounts for more than 733,000 franchise establishments in over 300 different business format categories, which support nearly 7.6 million jobs and $674.3 billion of economic output for the U.S. economy. Additionally, around 30% of franchise businesses are minority-owned, compared to less than 20% of non-franchised businesses.
Over the years, the franchise community has collaborated with public officials to shape the laws and policies that govern franchising, and have consistently supported regulatory policies designed to ensure that prospective franchisees receive relevant and material information about their proposed franchise purchases sufficiently in advance of such purchases to enable them to make informed and unpressured purchase decisions. Specifically, franchisors and franchisees alike continue to support a proper balance between the legitimate disclosure needs of prospective franchisees and compliance burdens and costsborne by both franchisors and franchiseesthat such disclosure inevitably entails. 
Just as many in the franchise community supported the FTCs early initiatives in the disclosure area in 1978 and the Rules modification in 2007, I strongly endorse continuation of the Rule in substantially its current format. The current Rule provides an adequate, minimum threshold for disclosing relevant and valuable information to prospective franchisees in considering the cost and nature of the proposed investment in advance of their franchise acquisition decisions, minimizing the potential for franchisors to misrepresent the health of their systems at the expense of franchisees. Much more, the Rule establishes a predictable, transparent, and understandable process that both franchisors and franchisees have become familiar, which prospective franchisees have come to expect, and with which franchisors have become increasingly compliant.
The absence of such information in the franchisees decision-making process would only lead to unacceptable levels of uninformed business decisions, distrust, investment losses, litigation, and additional government regulation, all of which would tarnish the reputation and integrity, and threaten the ever-growing economy- and life-enhancing benefits, of the franchise model itself. As now written, the Rule should be treated as inviolate and essential to the continued growth and success of the franchise model. I hope that the foregoing comments are helpful and express my appreciation for the FTCs role in preserving a trade regulation rule that contributes to the well-being of an essential and vibrant segment of the United States economy.
 
Respectfully submitted,
Shelly Sun, CEO and Founder of BrightStar Care
