Issues 1 & 2:
Yes, the Rule definitely helps the potential franchisee to get information about the franchise. One of the most valuable information is the contact for the existing franchisee in the system. It provides unbiased information that potential franchisee to access to.

Issues 3 a,b,c:
Modifications should be made

Suggestion One: Maintain a list of franchisees who left the franchise system in the last 10 years, with the following information:
- Franchisee First Name, and Last Initial
- Franchisee City and State
- Franchisee e-mail contact (at the time of separating from the system)
- Reason of leaving: terminated, transferred, non-renewal, purchased agreement but not open
- The year that franchisee joined the system
- The year that left the system
- Any litigation or arbitration history with the franchisee
- Non-disclosure statement signed or not
The franchisor is not responsible for maintaining the contact info to be current. But the franchisor must maintain this info in FDD until it passes 10 years mark. Therefore, it will not incur extra cost for the franchisor to maintain such a list in the FDD.
If there is any problem with the franchisor, those franchisees who left the system are more willing to share any bad experience. Even if those franchisees cannot share their experience, a long list of high turnover franchisees would indicate the franchisor problem of maintaining long term valuable franchisee. Also, an indication of the franchisor concentrate on profit from the initial franchise fee, rather than provide adequate supports to maintain long term franchise relationship.

Suggestion Two: Agree with both Lagarias, Napell & Dillon, LLP, and Witmer, Karp, Warner & Ryan LLP. "The Franchise Rule Should Prohibit Disclaimers of Additional Representations and of Reliance By Prospective Franchisees. This practice stands the Franchise Rule on its head and must end." I agree that the FTC should prohibit disclaimers in disclosure documents. Franchisor shall be responsible and liable for all information provided on the FDD, especially financial performance, cost and fees for buying and operating a franchise. No additional cost impact for the franchisor for removing disclaimers from FDD.

Suggestion Three: On item 19, prohibits franchisor to post store profits for just a group of selective stores. Posting profit for selective stores will definitely provide a skewed and deceptive picture. Instead, the franchisor should post stores average revenue (individually, in a group by geographic, or in total). Since most Franchisor has all the stores revenue (royalty usually calculated from % of revenue), Franchisor will be forced to report ALL stores, instead of pick and choose which stores to report. If a particular store revenue is not obtainable, it should be noted. And a count of how many stores do not report revenue should be provided. Minimal cost impact for the franchisor since franchisor should have this information in their system already.

Suggestion Four: On item 3, Litigation. Record of any litigation and arbitration related to the franchise should maintain for 3 years in the FDD in order for the potential franchisee to have easy access to this information. Minimal cost impact for the franchisor to maintain the last 3 years record.

Suggestion Five: A histogram of the years of experience of franchisee in the system should be provided in the FDD. The vertical axis shows the years of experience in the franchise system, from year 1 to year 10+. The horizontal axis shows the number of franchisee. Franchisee who left the system should also be counted in this statistic until it passes 10 years of history. Therefore, if there are a lot of short-timers in the system, it is easy to show in this histogram. The initial cost impact for franchisor this modification may be a concern. But once it is implemented, the continuation of maintaining such a record is minimal.

Issue 12:
Instead of franchisee address and phone number listed on the FDD, personal e-mail contact would be more appropriate to list. Franchisee most likely does not want to expose personal information on the list. E-mail contact provides enough privacy protection for a franchisee.

Summary: Norms and guiding principles for better business practices do not develop in a vacuum. At times they are brought about through the individual efforts of pioneering businesses that demonstrate a commitment to a higher standard. More often, they are grown through the hard work of the business community engaging collectively with the challenging questions presented by new technologies, new markets, or new societal challenges in order to build effective and accountable self- regulatory solutions. This is as true on the international stage as it is for the U.S. business community. U.S. leadership in the area of self-regulation has often paved the way toward the development of standards recognized by international bodies. Direct industry cooperation across borders has also been an effective tool. Although industry cooperation and self-regulation are usually initiated without government involvement, they are made more potent and durable by the support and encouragement of expert government actors like the FTC.

In considering the value of COPAs for patients and the healthcare system, please consider the academic research on Certificate of Need regulations, which is another state-based regulatory approach intended to control healthcare prices and improve quality. Like COPA laws, some state regulators support CON with the belief that government regulation reduces unnecessary duplication of healthcare resources and controls healthcare costs.
 I began studying CON regulations several years ago with a favorable attitude, because I believed that concentrating complex surgical operations at a smaller number of high-volume hospitals would build greater expertise and therefore better outcomes for patients. In 2009, I published a study that compared the experience of 7 states that dropped CON for open heart surgery and cardiac catheterization to states that maintained the regulations over the period 1989 to 2002 (Ho et. al., Health Services Research 2009). We found that states that dropped CON for cardiac care witnessed a 14% increase in the number of hospitals performing open heart surgery and a 12% rise in the number of hospitals providing cardiac catheterization relative to states that kept CON. As the total number of procedures was spread out over more facilities, the average volume of open heart surgeries and cardiac caths dropped roughly 30% in states that dropped CON rules, relative to states that maintained them. Nevertheless, there was no difference in mortality for cardiac care patients in states that dropped CON versus those that kept the regulations. In states that dropped CON, patients were able to choose from more facilities, without any increased risk of mortality.
 I published a study in 2012 that compared the cost consequences for the same 7 states that dropped CON regulations for cardiac care versus states that maintained the regulations (Ho and Ku-Goto, Medicare Care Research and Review 2012). We found that states that dropped CON experienced lower costs per patient for CABG but not for percutaneous coronary intervention. Average Medicare reimbursement was lower for both procedures in states that dropped CON. The cost savings from removing CON regulations slightly exceed the total fixed costs of new CABG facilities that entered after deregulation. Taken together these two studies imply that CON regulations are not justified in terms of either improving quality or controlling cost growth.
 These findings are supported by more recent studies that have concluded that removing CON for home health would have negligible systemwide effects on health care costs and quality (Polsky et. al. Journal of Public Economics 2014), and that CON laws have no statistically significant effect on allcause mortality (Bailey, Health Services Research 2018). Well-intentioned state CON regulations have not improved patient outcomes or lowered costs for patients. Healthy market competition amongst hospitals is a better strategy for improving patient welfare.

Bailey J., The Effect of Certificate of Need Laws on AllCause Mortality, Health Services Research, 2018; 53(1): 49-62.

Ho V, Ku-Goto MH, Jollis JG. Certificate of Need (CON) for cardiac care: controversy over the contributions of CON. Health Services Research, 2009; 44(2 Pt 1): 483-500.

Ho V, Ku-Goto MH. State deregulation and medicare costs for acute cardiac care. Medical Care Research and Review, 2013; 70(2): 185-205.

Polsky D, David G, Yang J, Kinosian B, Werner RM, Journal of Public Economics, 2014; 110:1-14.

In preparation for the consolidation of Level I Trauma services, the hospital administration gathered the data for comparison between Holston Valley Medical Center and Johnson City Medical Center. The data was to demonstrate the value of Holston Valley Medical Center as a Level I Trauma Center. Bishop & Associates was to use the data in their determination of which location to retain Level I Trauma Services at after the merger. It is not known if this material was provided to Bishop & Associates; only that hospital administration acquired this data and it was to be shared with them for their consultation. Per Ballad Health, Bishop & Associates determined that Johnson City Medical Center was the best 
location to retain the Level I Trauma services.

23 Counties in Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia were compared to determine the best location to retain Level I Trauma services based on driving time. With trauma, the first 60 minutes are critical to survival. Referred to as the golden hour, these 60 minutes are often the determining factor in a patients outcome. In this data, the drive times are compared and assigned a weighted score. (The lower the number the better.)

Only 8 of 23 Counties are within 60 Minute Drive Time to Johnson City Medical Center.

11 of 23 Counties are within 60 Minutes Drive Time to Holston Valley Medical Center. 

Weighted Scores (the lower the better): 
Holston Valley Medical Center: 542.22
Johnson City Medical Center: 585.10

As demonstrated by the numbers, Holston Valley is more accessible to the majority of the service region in receiving life-saving Level I Trauma Care within the critical golden hour - 60 minutes. 

This data is the most disturbing as it effectively demonstrates the conscious choice by Ballad Health to choose the facility where the least amount of people can get access to Level I Trauma care when they live exactly 60 minutes from the facility. These numbers do not include the population that lives more than or less than 60 minutes drive time from the facility, but rather ONLY 60 minutes.

12 out of 23 counties had a portion of their population exactly 60 minutes from Holston Valley Medical Center totaling 84,147 people. 6 out of 23 counties had a portion of their population exactly 60 minutes from Johnson City Medical 
Center totaling 17,750 people. 

By choosing Johnson City Medical Center as the location for the Level I Trauma services, Ballad Health Administration knowingly and intentionally chose to exclude 84,147 people from accessing Level I Trauma care within the critical, life-saving 60 minutes (golden hour). 

The data is conclusive and alarming given Ballad Healths decision to downgrade Holston Valley Medical Center to a Level III Trauma Center and retain Johnson City Medical as the only Level I Trauma Center in a region servicing 29 counties and 1.2 million people. 

DISCLAIMER: This is a personal interpretation of the data. I am not employed by nor do I represent Ballad Health, Bishop & Associates, or any other organization. I am a private citizen advocating for access to quality healthcare.

Johnson City Medical Center will be the only Level 1 trauma hospital and the Niswonger Childrens hospital will be the primary NICU. The downgrade is absurb considering Eastman and Domtar are within a 2 to 10 minutes drive. The "golden hour" is called such for a very good reason. This was vitally important to me over the last 10 years since I was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2010.At that time, I chose an oncologist with the Kingsport Hematology-Oncology group with the knowledge that I would use Holston Valley Hospital for any in-patient care. I must mention that I live in Carter County, Tennessee, which is approximately 25 miles from Kingsport, TN. Thankfully, my care during my battle with cancer was excellent and I am a healthy 70 year old survivor. During the 1 1/2 years of treatment in 2010 and 2011, I was hospitalized 6 times and had many visits to the emergency room. The difference in quality of care at Holston Valley Medical Center and my previous experiences, both personal and with family and friends, at the Johnson City Medical Center were at opposite ends of the spectrum. Following completion of treatments for breast cancer, which included 38 radiation treatments at HVMC's Christine LaGuardia Radiation Center, I have had several instances to use Wellmont services and have continued to see my oncologist at Kingsport Hem-Onc.

In my opinion, as a former ETSU Assistant Clinical Professor of Pediatrics staffing a MSHA-now-Ballad facility in Virginia, the Ballad Health COPA has been nearly criminally mismanaged and very poorly overseen by the states of Tennessee and Virginia - to the wholesale detriment of Ballad and ETSU clinical/other employees and patients alike. The lack of foresight is simply staggering. Based on my experience on his front lines, Alan Levine is a corporate menace who has repeatedly lied to the public about his intentions/methods, and whose leadership fosters an openly hostile and abusive-of-clinical employees work environment in his pursuit of complete domination/monopolization of an entire regions medical resources - FOR MONEY. Communication is utterly horrible and internal accountability of management is virtually non-existent. Retaliation is ingrained in the culture. I lived it. And I spoke out against it before almost anyone else. 

The attached letter is a modified/updated version of the letter I submitted to the Ballad Health COPA Committee at a hearing in Blountville, Tennessee on 2/7/2019. I spent eight hours on-the-road (traveling to and from my home in NC) to make my statement and submit the letter. 

I have yet to receive any kind of follow-up or response from either the Tennessee/Virginia Departments of Health or Attorneys General. I believe that this is because the state of Tennessee is downplaying its own liability both within and without the framework of the COPA. The state of Tennessee is obliged to defend the actions of ETSU no matter how heinous or how they might fly in the stated intent of the COPA. The Commonwealth of Virginia unfortunately appears to be just along for the ride. 

Erik Bodin (at the Virginia Department of Health) has much to answer for in terms of institutional enforcement of Virginia statute to protect a medical whistle-blower who has begged for his help for over 18 months. 

I have also presented a significant conflict-of-interest in terms of the CMS assessment of the second potential EMTALA violation I reported as CMS investigators based in Virginia worked for the former MSHA Regional Medical Director who helped recruit me to JMH and who, in conjunction with former ETSU Pediatric Chairman, David Wood, botched the negotiated terms of my ETSU/MEAC contracts.

Given the nature of the problems I reported . . . most specifically blatant sex/age discrimination on the part of East Tennessee State University (in deference to MSHA-now-Ballads openly hostile/abusive and retaliatory work environment), and #2 potential EMTALA violations (which threatened the lives of two infants) the second incident featuring a violation of Virginia Code 8.01-581.17,H on the part of Johnston Memorial/MSHA-now-Ballad executives (i.e. no employer shall take retaliatory action against an employee who in good faith makes a report of a patient safety date to a patient safety organization) . . . I find the good-faith oversight of the Ballad Health COPA to be significantly lacking. The states have created an inter-jurisdictional nightmare in which established state and Federal mechanisms of employee redress have little or no chance of working.

I believe that Wellmont-MSHA assets should not be merged in any kind of permanent fashion until clinical employees of both Ballad and ETSU are afforded adequate protections of time, livelihood and health under the COPA. 

It is my hope that the Federal government will now take a much more active role in STOPPING the finalization of this merger - and bringing more scrutiny to bear to the entire process/operation. An outside/Federal review of any/all downgrades (particularly of Neonatal, Pediatric and Trauma services) free of the incestuous/conflicted interests that have plagued this endeavor since its conception (by the self-described Hole-in-the-Wall-Gang") is imperative.

I thank the FTC for its attention and the opportunity to share my story. Ballad Health did not listen. I hope you do.

Mary H. Johnson, M.D., FAAP

Citizens of Northeast Tennessee and Southwest VA have been staging an around the clock protest in front of Ballad-Holston Valley Medical Center, Kingsport TN, for 44 days. After 6 months of emails and phone calls to the TN Dept of Health, the TN attorney general, and local politicians, we felt we had no choice but to try to garner regional and national attention in order to save our healthcare. 

The COPA between the State of Tennessee and Ballad Health, has destroyed our local healthcare. We no longer have quick access to emergency care and the quality of that care is significantly worse than it was before Ballad took over. Costs have increased, and life saving medications once available, are no longer. Competition has been displaced which puts us at the mercy of Ballad Health. At one time, Holston Valley Medical Center was nationally known for our heart center. Now, those same doctors and nurses that created that center, have quit. 

The quality of our Level One trauma center, that took years to build, is being stripped down to a level three. HVMC is centrally located in the Ballad service area. It has several access roads that ensure that if one road to HVMC is closed, an alternative can be quickly chosen. It has multiple helicopter landing pads and a reputation that was well known before Ballad took over. Since the takeover, two of our 3 trauma surgeons have quit, and one will be going on maternity leave soon. She doesn't plan to return. Doctors, nurses, and even the pharmacist in trauma have quit. The trauma center must rely on locum tenems, none which are in network. This has caused wait times to increase exponentially. Patients are given IV's and blood pressure cuffs, and sent back out to the lobby. Coming in by ambulance is no guarantee that you will be seen as an emergency. My son has attended feeding therapy and occupational therapy at the Laughlin Memorial Hospital pediatric rehab group (a Ballad Health facility in Greeneville, TN) for almost 2 years. What we were not told (and the rehab group staff were not told, either) is that the prices would be going up at the same time. For every weekly visit for the 2 years we've been there, we have self-paid $52 for feeding therapy (since our insurance doesn't cover it), and were billed $105.60 for the OT (the amount after insurance is billed). This may seem like a minor inconvenience, but for children like my son who have feeding and sensory issues, and borderline autism, it is life-altering.

MaineHealth, a non-profit charitable health care system headquartered in Portland, Maine, submits the attached comment letter in response to the Federal Trade Commission's ("Commission" or "FTC") request for comments in connection with the Commission's Certificate of Public Advantage ("COPA") Assessment Project and the June 18, 2019 workshop on the impact of COPAs.

The comment letter describes the background to and actual experience of MaineHealth in connection with a transaction approved under Maine's Hospital Cooperation Act.

 We are a poor area, huge#s of uninsured, disabled, mental health & drug affected. Our area is much like the "Island model" described in the after-action report of the Las Vegas Mass shooting ,in that our mountainous topography, inclement weather and sparse quality infrastructure make us extremely vulnerable to having ALL of our CURRENTLY available hospitals overwhelmed in the event of a mass cas or multiple traumas. Centralization of services is a BAD idea here. There is ONE road connecting Kingsport and Johnson City, ONE. 
 Allandale Infusion Center is closed= INCREASED travel distance to the new Ballad facility increases the cost to the patient. SIMILAR BUT NOT THE ORDERED/MOST EFFECTIVE DRUGS are being substituted which have increased the cost TO THE PATIENT, of a single treatment from about $3600 to over $13K. A patient was switched to ANOTHER drug which runs about $51K per treatment and has suffered a decline in health! The chairs in the new facility LACK CALL BUTTONS=SAFETY ALERT! 
The sewage system appears to have been poorly designed as already nauseous patients have to endure the smell of an unkempt outhouse AND they NOW get an ADDITIONAL $241 FACILITY FEE EVERY TIME THEY ENTER THE BLDG! Due to Medically Unnecessary transports BECAUSE OF STAFFING LOSSES, patients are shipped to multiple facilities incurring a charge for each! Insurance does NOT cover these! Then there are the exorbitant Telehealth FACILITY Fees-$31,$51,$53 for not even being there! ALL of these are NEW fees patients are responsible for as Insurance doesn't cover. Ballad sued one family over $11K bill which is why TN is #1 in Medical Bankruptcy!
2. Monitoring the COPA: Well, IF it was being monitored MAYBE we would know! The TN DoH just said they had NOT obtained "enough data" FROM Ballad to say if Ballad was even in compliance with the terms of the COPA-until 2020!

Facility Fee:

Previously, patients were given the medication prescribed by their physician regardless of its costs and if the patient was inpatient or outpatient. Ballad Health has changed this practice.

I recently attended the FTC workshop entitled A Health Check on COPAs held in Washington D.C. on June 18, 2019. My take aways from this workshop are as follows:

 There is no clear and convincing evidence that COPAs have succeeded in improving quality of care, access to services, 
 or lowering patient costs
 That the creation of a health care monopoly, more often than not, is detrimental to the public it is supposed to serve
 That even where studies have been attempted to definitively define advantages vs. disadvantages, the data needed to 
 make such determinations is often incomplete, unavailable, or deficient
 That once a COPA is granted it must forever require oversight to ensure that monopolistic practices do not 
 disadvantage the public
 In the absence of oversight an unregulated monopoly results
 COPAs are risky adventures and should only be granted after extensive factual investigation has been conducted

With regard to the Ballad Health COPA, panelist and Deputy Attorney General for the State of Tennessee, Janet Kleinfelter, stated unequivocally that after 16 months of operation the State was unable to determine if the COPA was working properly. She further stated that it may take 3, 4, or 5 years of operation before the state could adequately determine if the COPA was placing citizens at a disadvantage with regard to quality of care, access to care, and cost of services.

In my judgment, this amounts to an admission that the State has created a health care monopoly that is out of control. The State has not done due diligence in having in place necessary controls and indices to effectively oversee the monopoly they have created.

In other words, the State has failed to protect the public from what has become a coercive monopoly by Ballad Health. In my opinion, this amounts to regulatory negligence and warrants federal intervention by the FTC or DOJ to determine if federal antitrust laws have been violated.

Full comments in attached filing -- along with White Paper outlining privacy regulations and actions regarding technology. 

We appreciate the opportunity to submit this comment to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) as it evaluates the direction of competition and consumer protection enforcement and policy in the 21st Century. Throughout these hearings, some participants wrongly suggested that the FTC should revise or otherwise supplement its regulation of the technology industry, particularly in the areas of privacy, data security, and competition. When evaluating these recommendations, we urge the Commission to reject these proposed changes and recognize the robust regulatory frameworks that apply to the technology industry today.

NetChoice is a trade association of leading e-commerce and online companies promoting the value, convenience, and choice of internet business models. Our mission is to make the internet safe for free enterprise and for free expression. We work to promote the integrity and availability of the global internet and are significantly engaged in privacy issues in the states, in Washington, and in international internet governance organizations.

With this comment, we submit a white paper that describes the myriad ways in which the technology industry is highly regulated across a myriad of issue areas, including in the competition and consumer protection contexts. Specifically, we describe the extensive regulatory frameworks that govern how technology companies interact with consumers, manage content, and conduct themselves in the market. We begin with a high level overview of the laws, regulations, and other requirements that apply to technology companies and are enforced by federal agencies, state officials, and private litigants across the country. We then provide a more detailed outline of these authorities, case examples, and other information that will aid the Commission in assessing the existing regulatory landscape.

Our analysis provides details on the many substantive areas that regulations of technology companies address.

In the attached, first we identify the federal and state consumer protection, privacy, and data security laws, regulations, self-regulatory programs, and other authorities that govern how technology companies interact with consumers. For example, we describe how the FTC uses its Section 5 authority to bring enforcement actions against technology companies for alleged unfair and deceptive practices, including in the areas of privacy and data security, and how states attorneys general bring similar law enforcement actions. We explain how federal agencies issue and enforce regulations of digital practices based on sectoral laws, and outline more general consumer protection authorities that govern, among other things, advertising, adware and spyware, online disclosures, and endorsements.

Second, we identify federal laws and regulations that impose liability or otherwise put regulatory pressure on technology companies with respect to the content on their platforms. For example, we describe how federal copyright laws impose direct and secondary liability on platforms for allegedly infringing copyright or facilitating the infringement of copyright on their platforms. We also describe how platforms are subject to robust notice and takedown requirements, and how recent legal developments have expanded technology companies potential exposure to liability for user-generated content on their platforms.

Third, we outline the federal and state laws, regulations, and guidelines that restrict how technology companies conduct themselves in the market. For example, we describe how federal agencies regulate antitrust in the U.S. through laws such as the Sherman Antitrust Act, the FTC Act, and the Clayton Act, among others, and how state officials supplement this authority by bringing enforcement actions under their own versions of federal antitrust and unfair competition laws. We also discuss how private litigants provide enforcement efforts by bringing private antitrust cases against companies in the technology industry, and how patent laws have placed additional constraints on technology companies practices.

In sum, we urge the Commission to recognize the comprehensive legal framework that currently protects consumers and other businesses while allowing the Internet to grow and power the economy. If, despite the panoply of laws, rules, and enforcements discussed in the attached paper, the FTC decides to pursue new regulations, those new regulations must solve a problem and specific harm to consumers or other businesses, and avoid causing collateral damage that will impact the U.S.s longstanding position as the leader in technology innovation.

I am writing to share with the Federal Trade Commission a report on big data that I recently submitted to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) on behalf of Google LLC (Google). Although it was prepared in response to concerns raised by the ACCC, the report discusses in detail a number of subjects that have also been raised during the FTCs recent Hearings on Competition and Consumer Protection in the 21st Century, particularly regarding the role of data in digital platform competition and the conditions under which the utilization of data might create barriers to entry and expansion. It is my hope that the enclosed report will be helpful to the FTC in considering these important issues.

My report was occasioned by questions raised in the ACCCs ongoing Digital Platforms Inquiry. In the context of that inquiry, the ACCC asked commenters for their views on whether data-driven network effects and economies of scale may give established digital platforms that possess large amounts of data an enduring competitive advantage. With regard to Google, the ACCCs Preliminary Report explored whether Google is insulated from dynamic competition by barriers to entry and expansion for search platforms... arising from network effects, including network effects that supposedly flow from the collection and utilization of user data. The ACCC explored whether Facebook is insulated from dynamic competition for similar reasons. 

As I explain in my report, I believe the answer to these questions is no. In my view, neither network effects nor the collection and utilization of user data prevent entry or competition from search rivals. With respect to network effects, search services are typically not characterized by either same-side or cross-side network effects. And, with regard to data, there is no economic evidence indicating that access to a large volume of user data is necessary to compete effectively.

I describe the evidence supporting these conclusions in the attached letter.

The second set of proposed new Regulations to be added to the Contact Lens Rule differs in substance very little from the first set of proposed new regulations. In other words it is still very deeply flawed, unnecessary, and onerous to optometrists and ophthalmologists. 

The Spectacle Rule has been in effect since the 1970's, ie, for over 40 years, and during that time NO ONE has suggested that doctors be required to have patients sign a form that says they have a received a copy of their spectacle prescription and that they have right to fill that prescription somewhere else. The reason that no one has suggested this is because there is nothing in the spectacle industry equivalent to 1-800-Contacts and it's allies in the contact lens industry. The Contact Lens Rule has only been in effect since 2003, and yet this proposal was brought up in 2016. It was brought up despite a lack of any evidence that there has been any problem with patients being able to obtain their prescriptions for contact lenses. Very few complaints have been received by the FTC during this time despite hundreds of millions of prescriptions being written, and about half of the complaints that were received had nothing to do with prescription release.

!-800-Contacts and their allies want this because they have found that doctors have no problem matching the prices at 1-800-Contacts, thus taking away any incentive for patients to order their contact lenses from 1-800-Contacts. additionally, doctors have the ability to carry contact lenses in stock for convenient same day pick up. And some doctors have their own mail order services for patients. All of these free market factors have combined to create a situation where 1-800-Contacts has nothing unique or better to offer to the patients. The free market is working as it is intended to! Thus 1-800-Contacts is pushing a government regulation designed to get patients to stop buying their contact lenses from their doctors. 

The government is not supposed to be intervening on behalf of a big business to help it compete against many tens of thousands of small businesses. That is not a free market situation! But that is exactly what the purpose of this new regulation is: to help the mail order contact lens industry, an industry with a long and sordid history of violating the laws and ignoring standards of care. 

Regarding other parts of this new set of proposed regulations, there is a section that allows the seller to change the brand of the contact lenses being sold if the patient is informed. This should never be allowed. Contacts are fit based on the lens material, the base curves, and the diameters, not just the lens powers. This fitting process takes place between the doctor and the patient. After fitting the contact lenses, follow-up is performed to make sure that the lenses are working well and not causing any eye heath problems. If the seller is allowed to change the brands after the fact, there is no refitting or follow up being done! This is ridiculous and should never be permitted. 

Many legislators in Congress, both in the Senate and the House, have spoken out against these proposed new regulations. Despite all of the opposition from the legislators themselves, the FTC has done nothing more than mildly modify the regulations that it originally proposed. It is time to rethink these regulations from the beginning. It has been proposed that a sign in the doctors office could be used instead. This is certainly as far as any further regulation should go, especially from an administration that prides itself on cutting, not increasing regulations.

As many have stated, the current design of loot boxes has all the hallmarks of gambling, be it lottery tickets, slot machines, etc. The same thrills, risks, and potential for addictive behavior. There is no need for me to reiterate that here.

I'm proposing an amicable solution and debunking a comparison. Some equate loot boxes to currently existing in products not seen as gambling such as packs of baseball cards, another product that is aimed at a market including children. Baseball cards have a strong secondary market allowing the consumer to find individual items and pay what is deemed market price for those specific items. Also, the secondary market allows the consumer to sell or trade their unwanted cards at what is deemed market price for those items. The majority of current game Loot boxes do not allow for a secondary market of their items, and virtually none of them allow for real money sales of their digital items. Not that I am advocating for that, just pointing out the large distinction between the current loot box economy and baseball cards and the like is the lack of a secondary market giving value to the items purchased. The creation of a secondary market for these digital items creates more issues than it solves, and that shouldn't be the path forward. From a consumer protection standpoint, we should want to make all the risks clear and visible from the start as well as making the undesired items purchased from loot boxes not worthless without creating a real money secondary market.

To that end, here is my set of recommendations: All Loot Boxes should have the odds of receiving an item of certain rarities very clearly marked before and after purchase. i.e., this Loot Box has a 1:4 chance of getting a rare item, a 1:9 chance of getting an elite item, and a 1:100 chance of getting a legendary item. Also, no item within a specific rarity should be any more or less likely to be obtained than any other item of that rarity. i.e., a specific legendary item should not be any harder to get from a Loot Box than any other legendary item. Every game that has Loot Boxes will be required to allow the exchange of any item found in the Loot Boxes by trading in no more than 5 items of the same rarity of the desired item received from those Loot Boxes. i.e., a game has Loot Boxes and the elite rarity is a 1:9 drop from the Loot Box, Player A has obtained 5 elite rarity items from Loot Boxes, Player A must be able to trade those 5 elite rarity items from Loot Boxes to receive any 1 specific elite rarity item possible from that Loot Box that they want in exchange. The game will have the option of lowering that number if so desired, but they cannot require more than 5 items of that rarity to be traded in exchange for another specific item of that rarity. Lastly, to ensure there is a way around the gambling aspect of Loot Boxes every item available in a Loot Box that is purchased with cash must also be purchasable by cash and also display the estimated cost to acquire the item by buying Loot Boxes and trading in game at the in game ratio (no higher than 5 to 1) for that item. i.e., using the 1:100 chance of getting a legendary item and the game has chosen to stick to the 5 items required to trade in and that the Loot Boxes cost $1 each, the Estimated Price to Acquire a specific legendary item would be $500 (1:100 so on average 100 $1 Loot Boxes needed to get 1 legendary item, then you would need 5 legendary items to trade in for this specific one.) and that $500 Estimate to Acquire via Loot Boxes would be required to be shown on the item page to purchase the item. The price the game decides to charge in cash for the item without purchasing the Loot Boxes will also be displayed on this page and that price is to be determined by the game company. Also, game companies will not be required to exchange any number of lesser rarity items to equal a higher rarity item. They may do so if desired, but that will not be required. i.e., even though the pack says 1:100 legendary it does not mean the game has to let you trade 100 common items for a legendary.

This reduces risks for consumers and puts both a clear price of plainly purchasing the item and the estimated price it would cost if you tried your luck with the Loot Boxes in front of the consumer from the start and explains the risks to the consumer then. It also provides the consumers with value for their unwanted items. From the game company standpoint, this is a much better solution than creating a real money secondary market and all the issues that will cause. This also allows game companies to continue with this practice in a way that is not as harmful to the consumer. It would still need to be regulated to avoid minors from being able to engage in the Loot Boxes with real money, but allowing them to purchase the item for cash if allowed by state and federal laws and agreed upon from their parents or guardians per the game's EULA.

Thanks for your time.

The proposal to have the seller verify only the contact lens brand or manufacturer is problematic for a few reasons, most of which would be anti-competitive and ultimately result in higher prices for consumers. 

The crux of the issue is that some contact lenses may be similar to the prescribed brand and have the same/similar material properties, base curve, diameter and thickness but have a different brand name or manufacturer. Under this scenario, a seller would not be able to offer this 'generic' brand as it may not be explicitly requested by consumer (the customer may not know this brand is an option or the manufacturer). This provides an advantage to the established, higher priced brands despite broad similarity to alternative offerings. This is akin to restricting generic medicines in favor of only established, branded medicines - something that is not in the interest of consumers and health care costs in America.

Perhaps a more sensible and consumer friendly approach would be to verify prescriptions according to material and/or base curve and diameter. Whilst not perfect, it would allow more competition in the lens market and leave it up to the consumer to decide which lenses fit according to their preference and budget (albeit there should be flexibility to change material if desired). Alternatively, an equivalency based on material used can also be established based on FDA data for various lens brands registered by the FDA. This would level the playing field instead of limiting consumer options to just a brand name. It is quite apparent that this section of the draft proposal mostly benefits the established players and eye care professionals at the expense of consumers. Furthermore, it is well known that a handful of lens manufacturers account for an outsized proportion of the contact lens market and have a vested interest in maintaining this market share. The current draft proposal only enables this further.

Finally, there is an element of scare mongering by eye care professionals against alternative 'generic' brands that has not been empirically proven in other markets. Other developed countries (ie in the European Union) allow consumers with prescriptions to purchase and try regulated and approved lens brands which may be broadly similar to see what works for them, with minimal adverse effects to date (ie if it doesn't work, customers discontinue). For example, a consumer should be able to switch from a higher priced silicon hydrogel lens to a more affordable hydrogel lens if they desire without much friction or additional costs. The ability to do this has resulted in more choice, better customer service, convenience and lower prices for consumers in the EU. Perhaps this is something that should be taken into consideration in light of the changes in technology that have enabled consumers to have more choice and control over their purchasing habits.

Consumers own their products and should have the right to repair them as they wish. In conclusion, as consumers we should have the right to repair our own goods, including our electronics. We own them, we should be able to repair them. The ability to repair gives consumers an expanded skillset that would lead to a more robust job market. For the safety of our environment we need to reduce our electronic waste, which the ability to repair our electronics would provide.

My name is Kevin Kenney and I am an AG Engineer '86 (BS-UNL). I've worked at Southwest Research Institute - Locomotive Test Center San Antonio, TX performing patent research on fuel for internal combustion that lower emissions. I am holder of multiple patents for multi-fuel options for diesel engines. (Patent numbers:#9441560/September 13, 2016 & 8826888/September 9, 2014) 

My area of expertise is in diesel engine tuning for the purpose of lowering emissions - specifically substituting 'High Octane' clean alcohols (ethanol & methanol) and gaseous fuels (propane & natural gas) in place of diesel fuel. My customers are farmers. I know many of the local technicians working for both company dealerships (with repair software) and independent mechanics (without software). I have also been actively involved with the Nebraska Farm Bureau, testing of biofuels "Ethanol used in Diesel Engines" at University of Nebraska, Lincoln at the Tractor Testing Lab and multiple other activities biofueled/diesel projects. 

Government Affairs representatives from AEM/EDA filed comments taking the position that the only reason Farmers & Ranchers want Right to Repair legislation is to hack their emissions to avoid EPA Tier 4 emissions compliance. The implication is that farmers are trying to harm the environment which is both insulting and factually unsupported. 

My experience with farmers tells me that farmers would far prefer to use cleaner fuel than diesel and are frustrated by OEM created software limitations on engines that restrict the use of cleaner options. My patents would allow such options so I have paid very close attention to this issue. 

The US Copyright Office made software tuning legal in 2016 and expanded the opportunity in 2018 for farmers to hire experts, such as myself, to deliver fuel tuning options they prefer. While the USCO has made hacking technically legal, the practical ability to do so remains blocked in the same way as owner-directed repair. Manufacturers have not made any software, manuals schematics, diagnostics, parts or tools available to the owner, functionally blocking owner control of tunes as well as of repair. 

Independents techs need the same information made available to dealer techs to help farmers legally Modify or hack their tractors. Without capabilities to retune and re-tune existing firmware and software settings, these tractors will remain belching dirty diesel fuel for the rest of their lives. Tellingly, CASE IH and AGCO both design and make propane and natural gas tractors for, "FOREIGN SALES ONLY" leaving US farmers stuck with diesel. 

My clients are only able to use clean fuels as an alternative to diesel by hacking/modding. We need the repair software to re-set codes and program/re-program existing engine control units (ECUs) capable of operating with different specs but not yet accessible with manufacturer limitations. Yet farmers seeking to tune their engines do not have the same options as owners of over-the-road vehicles are doing under existing Right to Repair voluntary agreements where software is available. 

In response to the AEM/EDA survey posted as empirical data - I did my own survey calling my 'Hacker Buddies' (roughly a dozen techs, 'Hackers' & enthusiasts that specialize in engine ECU work). They laughed at the AEM/EDA survey's calculation of the percentage of modified (Hacked) tractors. Their experience is the percent of hacked tractors is extremely low - maybe 1-5% with 5% being extremely unlikely at the high end.

Dealers undoubtedly see modified or hacked equipment in their service bays where they wouldnt likely be able to discern any of these purported emission 'Hacks' . When a tractor rolls in the shop it will appear normal unless the diesel particulate filter (DPF) was removed. Most common hacks don't leave a digital signature after the exhaust gas return (EGR) or diesel emission fluid (DEF) is adjusted nor do they leave an electronic signature on a horsepower tune. A dealer would have to put a tractor on a DYNO to prove such improvements which is both time consuming and costly. 

In the real world, I know of many "Tractor Hackers who work quietly for the dealership to help support their customers unofficially in ways that the dealership cannot. In my experience, nearly all Nebraska John Dealer dealerships have used outside 'Tractor Hackers' one way or the other based on my exposure to this scenario. Dealerships want to help their customers, and if they need to call in a 'Hacker Buddy' to fix and/or modify their 'Electronic Junk' they will. You'd be surprised as to how many service managers order these 'Hacks'....

Please let me know if you have any questions or if I can be of service. 

Yours Truly,

Kevin Kenney
R2R Advocate for Farmers & Ranchers
AG Engineer '86 (BS-UNL)
Raymond, Nebraska

Greetings,

Loot boxes are many things. They represent gambling in video games, they offer developers an alternative revenue stream, they give gamers a sense of progression, and sometimes they can represent pay to win mechanics where the person with the fattest wallet comes out on top. 

With respect to your workshop, I genuinely believe that video game companies are exploiting the predatory side of loot boxes. This being the gambling side of things. Certain companies (Blizzard) have limited time events where special outfits and voice lines can be unlocked for your characters. This encourages people to spend money on more and more loot boxes in pursuit of that one skin they really like. In the case of children with access to a credit card, hundreds, potentially thousands can be spent.

Ultimately, I believe in little to no regulation, but children and vulnerable people are being targeted here by these so called surprise mechanics (as if this were a kinder egg or a childrens toy). And these video games are profiting off of people who cant control themselves. Casinos are regulated, lotteries are regulated, and ultimately, so should loot boxes. 

Thank you for your time,
Dillon Sloat

Loot boxes should not be regulated as they are not gambling. To be gambling, there must be an intrinsic monetary value to the award that is received through luck, however with loot boxes, these items cannot be exchanged for money and are tied to the account being used, therefore there is no monetary value. Furthermore, in the vast majority of games that use loot boxes, the items in the loot boxes can be earned by playing the game normally; the loot boxes serve simply as a way to unlock these items faster should the player choose. Loot boxes do not restrict the player's ability to play the game and simply serve a cosmetic function, changing either an in game weapon's skin or a character's skin, or adding some sort of visual effect. As there is no game mechanic altering function in loot boxes, nor is there an intrinsic monetary value to the items in loot boxes therefore making it not a form of gambling, there should be no government regulation on the topic.

The ESA and ESRB refuse to educate the public about lootboxes, going so far as to hide their "parental tools" behind hard to find websites or outright leaving any knowledge of lootboxes our of their ESRB rating system. Claims that their system is "the gold standard" are years old and have not been tested in this new environment. Simply put, the ESRB is failing to do what it was created to do -- protect and help consumers make informed decisions.

The video game industry does not do its due dilligence to educate its consumers on this issue despite numerous major outrages surrounding games such as Star Wars Battlefront. Rather than confront this issue ESA and companies such as EA have used new words to describe them, such as "surprise mechanics" and continually avoid the discussion. 

Further the World Health Organization has labeled video games as addictive and if gambling is also addictive, and video games are using gambling mechanics, why are we not researching more into this? Why are we allowing ESA and companies to stymie the ability for consumers to learn more and get the truth?

Lootboxes do not encourage innovation. They do not make games more fun for consumers. They are not clearly explained. Their odds are not published or even discussed, and they are absolutely marketed to children through influencers and other advertisements.They are gambling and there's no other way to describe it.

In addition to the form letter below, which I wholeheartedly agree with, I'd just say as an associate doctor in a small business private practice that the process of providing quality eye care services and products in this country is already unbelievably bureaucratic and burdensome. Andrew Brauer, OD

Dear Chairman Simons,

We are a husband and wife optometry team practicing in Thornton, Colorado. We started our practice in 2010 and see patients of all ages in a primary eye care setting. Our practice sees a large number of contact lens wearers, many of whom wear specialty, and medically-necessary contact lenses. We practice optometry to the highest standards, and in accordance with the American Optometric Associations standards of Professional Conduct, our primary ethical responsibility is to place our patients interests above our own. Recent news in our profession has brought several concerns to our attention that we would like to share with you.

Through the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act (FCLCA), Congress charged the FTC with enforcing contact lens prescription release. Despite eye doctors dutifully complying with their requirements under the law, the FTC has issued a proposed change to the Contact Lens Rule which would mandate that eye doctors meet new Confirmation of Prescription Release requirements, by retaining either a patient-signed document or, with patient consent, evidence that the prescription was delivered and made available electronically. Doctors would then be required to maintain compliance evidence for each contact lens patient for a period of three years and be able to produce this evidence in the event of a federal investigation.

The FTC proposal is being advanced despite FTCs own data showing that over a recent five-year period the Commission received a total of 309 consumer complaints out of roughly 200 million contact lens prescriptions issuedwith half of those complaints being unrelated to any violation of the Rule. The FTC estimates that the new mandate will cost the industry more than $13 million annually. Eye doctors have offered a proposed alternative backed by the National Consumers League (which is already law in California) to instead require the posting of signage informing patients of their rights under the law.

We firmly believe that the patient-doctor relationship should be less about bureaucracy, and more about addressing patient issues, instituting preventative eye health measures, and patient education than adding to an unneeded paperwork burden. Patients are aware that they can purchase their contact lenses anywhere they like with the contact lens prescription we provide to them, and filling out more forms over the matter doesnt benefit the patient. The additional time required for this unneeded paperwork would disrupt the patient-doctor relationship by communicating to the patients that they should be wary of their physician, and assume that their doctor is a violator of Federal law. Time that would otherwise be spent on patient care would be spent satisfying the misdirected aims of this requirement.

As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. 

Brian Abert, O.D.

Dear Chairman Simons,

I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in Brighton, Colorado. 

The proposed contact lens release paperwork is unnecessary and burdensome regulation. This is a solution to a problem which does not exist in any significant statistical measure. 
 
I have ALWAYS and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. 

Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. Here are active examples that I hope the agency is aware of: 

-Patients over Paperwork: CMS initiated this regulatory review in 2017 aimed at removing regulatory obstacles that get in the way of providers spending time with patients.

More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country.

As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. 

Rodney Fair, O.D.

Dear Chairman Simons,

I am a practicing doctor of optometry and the Government Relations Chair for Arizona Optometric Association. I was directly involved with the 2014 -2016 1-800 Contacts supported bills that were introduced in Arizona that would have taken contact lenses out of the realm of medical device and made them purely a commodity with no health protections or oversight. 

I have directly experienced the misleading statements and outright lies told by this company to the public and legislators solely for profit and with no regards to their eye health. Anyone you speak with will say that their eyesight is the most important sense to them and they would rather lose a limb or hearing rather than lose their sight. Our citizens deserve to have laws and rules in place to help them protect their eyesight.

I have directly witnessed 1-800 disregarding the current FTC regulations and have shipped lenses off of expired prescriptions to children underage a week before faxing my office for a verification. I myself have ordered lenses and received them for over a year (three times) for lenses that I have never been prescribed and were not even the powers of my submitted (by my eye doctor) Rx. I got lenses shipped to me in 2015 that were off an expired Rx from 2007. I have the boxes and the confirmations of shipment and their website showing a 2007 Rx only. Because my doctor responded to the verification request, they counted that as an approval and will ship for 2 years from receipt of an invalid Rx. These are blatant disregard for the 2003 rules that the rest of us abide by.

I see these proposed changes, which add additional burden on our offices, as a reward for bad behavior for a company that doesn't even follow the current set of Rules.

I am always surprised when 1-800 Contacts says that people don't realize that they can purchase lenses somewhere other than their doctors office. Really?! Their name...1-800-contacts...was their phone number in the 1990's before the internet that people called to order their contact lenses. EVERYONE knows that they can purchase lenses anywhere they want. Poor argument. 
How about we make sure that patients are getting the proper lenses and have regular evaluation of their ocular health no matter where they purchase their lenses.

Please show some common sense thinking and see through the misleading statements.

LEAVE THE RULE AS IT HAS BEEN since 2003.

Annette Hanian, O.D.

Hello, my name is Kyle Gould and I am a concerned citizen from New York State.

I am writing to urge the Federal Trade Commission to streamline the process for contact lens prescriptions as well as create regulations that make it so that contact lens bought online have to go through the same prescription process as regular contact lens purchases.

Optometrists have detailed that the current rules offer too much of a burden on providing contact lenses for patients. They claim that they do not have the ability to properly address patient needs. The FTC must take into account optometrist opinions and call on actual eye specialists and experts in the Department of Health and Human Services to gauge what is needed. 

The FTC must also create regulations on contact lenses purchased online. Without a health specialist to provide the needed information, people could fall prey to predatory practices by industry or purchase the wrong product for their individual needs. This is why all online purchases must be reviewed by optometrists before the purchases are made so that patients do not suffer from misinformation or even worse, getting products that may be detrimental to their eye health.

Kyle Gould

The Federal Trade Commission has a duty to protect users of consumer products including contact lenses. The debate for freer disclosure of prescriber results of ocular exams which help consumer buy the product at a competitive price has been going on for several decades.

It is always prudent that the disclosure statement is given to consumers through a duty of the prescriber to work in good faith and with complete candor. Some but not the majority of providers fail in this effort. It is a problematic situation since the FTC does not punish violators to a major extent rather it can issue cease and desist orders and argue investigative cases in federal and administrative courts.

The proposal to allow several new areas of disclosure and transmission of information will lead to a quicker response to consumer requests, help relieve a paperwork burden through electronic transmission, allows for more sellers to participate due to availability of prescription criteria, and creates uniformity throughout the network.

If there are bad actors working in this system, possibly the Commission could further educate consumers on how to file a complaint in writing, phone, e-mail, electronic means or through other prescribed avenues. Those that skirt the regulations will eventually be revealed through the complaint process and dealt with administratively.

This proposal is it becomes effective would be consistent with the public interest and with the policies previously released by the agency. There is no doubt that the modified Contact Lens Rule should be embraced by prescribers, sellers and consumers as an improvement to consumer products trade rules.

The Contact Lens Rule is in favor of not only the Optometrist but also the contact wearer. The Contact lens rule is there to show proof of supply and distribution of the correct product, which is considered a medical device. If there was something wrong with the contact, the supplier would be able to track how many people received the product. The Optometrist would be able to then contact his patients if needed. It could also be helpful in guarding the Optometrist against a civil action lawsuit if a patient said they received a wrong or damaged contact lense which may have injured them in anyway. Without this rule in place it might be easy for someone to say they did not receive the right contact lens perscription from their optometrist.

This rule seems to be an attempt to increase access to eye prescriptions while also making it easier and more efficient for prescribers to adhere to the Contact Lens Rule by allowing more flexible forms of signature from the patient. I support this ruling because I think each patient has a right to their own medical records. Whether they use those records to shop around to get a better price or it collects dust in a bin, the patient still has a right to that information. Im all in favor of prescribers being able to offer a digital alternative to the consent & record form as long as the cost of providing these alternatives do not outweigh the benefits or perceived harm from lessened competition.

As a practicing ophthalmologist, I am deeply concerned about proposals included in the Federal Trade Commission's proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule. This new burden is also unwarranted, as there is little evidence that ophthalmologists are not in compliance with the existing Contact Lens Rule. 

Such an administrative burden should not be placed on small businesses that are already going to great lengths to comply with the Contact Lens Rule and do so despite serious concerns with the current prescription-verification system that we believe puts our patients at risk. While we appreciate the FTC's effort in trying to alleviate additional burdens on physician practices by suggesting multiple avenues through which prescribers could comply with new requirements, the proposed changes will still place financial and administrative burdens on ophthalmology practices.I have had detailed discussions with our office manager about the work implications of your requirement for patient acknowledgement and filing for three years. FTC believes this adds only one minute extra work perpatient. We strongly disagree: we believe that this requirement will take an extra ten minutes per patients and subsequently will add an extra 850 man hours burden to our ophthalmology practice.
 
I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.

Based on evidence presented in the rule proposal, some consumers are not being presented with the option to retrieve their contacts from the seller of their choice or not being presented their prescriptions at all, which is a significant problem. We appreciate the opportunity to comment in this important proposed rule related to security of personal information. 

Regarding the added guidance on specific aspects of information security programs, we disagree with the proposed change because we understand that it may be derive in a tick the box mentality, which could be ineffective to the rapid changing environment of information security. We believe a better approach would be to incorporate non-mandatory guidance or best practices as published informative documents, not part of rulemaking. 

Regarding the added provisions for accountability, we agree with the proposed changes as it may create a greater sense of accountability for leadership of the financial institutions without generating burdensome requirements. 

Regarding the exemptions for small businesses, we agree with the proposed changes to alleviate the administrative burden for small business without significantly affecting public interest. 

Regarding the expanded definition of financial institution, we disagree with the proposed change as it may have unintended future consequences in the constantly changing economic environment potentially affecting new businesses. We think it would be preferable to specifically include finders in the definition of financial institution. 

Regarding the proposal to include the definition of financial institution and related examples in the Rule itself, we agree with the proposed change because it would provide with greater clarity about the scope of the Rule without generating any negative impact.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notice titled "Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information" and published in the Federal Register of April 4, 2019. The notice proposes changes to the Safeguards Rule that implements the Gramm-Bliley-Leach Act (the Act), The FTC majority stated in the notice (84 Fed. Reg. at 13170, col. 3) in reference to proposed 16 CFR 314.6: "This proposed section is intended to reduce the burden on smaller financial institutions." The two-member minority stated in dissent (84 Fed. Reg. 13177, col. 2): "The expansion of the Rule could create traps for the unwary, especially small and innovative businesses. Further, large incumbents can often absorb regulatory compliance costs more effectively than new entrants or smaller players, potentially decreasing competition." Thus, all FTC members agreed on the importance of not imposing undue burdens on small businesses.

 In this context, the proposed 16 CFR 314.6 intended to protect small businesses from undue burdens under the Safeguards Rule, I believe that the proposal in fact doesnt achieve the objective. As the proposed 16 CFR 314.6 exempts a financial institution that maintains "customer information concerning fewer than five thousand consumers" from some obligations to document its risk assessment, documenting the risk response plan, regularly update their assessment of risks, and exemption from having its CISO chief information security officer report yearly to the governing body. The proposal assumes that the only burden on a small business is because of the written reports and several assessments, but in fact, the rule imposes many burdens that do not take into account the size of small businesses. Also, the rule considered the number of consumers that the institution has to hold their information is dependent upon the size of the business and in fact, it does not. Accordingly, it is recommended to relate the number of employees/officers working in each institution with the administrative burdens imposed by the new rule.

(1) Whether the disclosure, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements are necessary, including whether the resulting information will be practically useful; 

In order to help consumers to make an educated decision and at the same time allow enforcement actions involving alleged misstatements on labels or in advertisements, disclosure, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements are necessary. One should not take away the consumer right of knowing the fact before purchase with the concern of extra cost burdened by the public. 
Given the data is accurate, it should help consumers to make an educated decision regardless of the ultimate choice one made. The data also help manufacturers to improve internally and compete externally which eventually will benefit consumers.

(2) the accuracy of our burden estimates, including whether the methodology and assumptions used are valid; 

The burden estimates based on the assumption that 25% of all basic models may not be robust and lead to inaccurate estimation of the total estimates. Given the manufacturers are able to provide the necessary data, they should also be able to provide the exact models being tested as part of their submission. Therefore, the exact testing burden hours of each model should be precise instead of estimates. 

(3) how to improve the quality, utility, and clarity of the disclosure requirements; and 

There should be a flag as a part of the data submission to signal if a specific model is being tested and so the testing burden hours should be as close to the actual hours as possible which can be calculated. The other disclosure requirements are clear as describe and necessary for the purpose.

(4) how to minimize the burden of providing the required information to consumers.

In order to minimize the burden of providing the required information to consumers, FTC can centralize testing, reporting, recordkeeping, and labeling requirements through a third party either directed by FTC or an industry governed association. Instead of having the manufacturers borne the cost individually, a fraction of the cost can be collected when a new model disclosure is submitted. Assuming most of the categories being tested are standardized appliances, the testing procedures should be combined and automated as much as possible.

I do believe that there are types of personal information that would be useful to operators to improve their products, and that they should be allowed to do so, since improved educational products would be beneficial to future students. I also believe there should be a limit, both in what types of information can be used and what it can be used for. Considering that the children in question are not yet old enough to give their own consent for the collection and use of such information, and the potential for any electronically gathered information to persist in databases for long periods of time is very real, its vitally important that the information only be allowed to be collected and used for any purpose if it can be de-identified and is general in nature such that it could not be reasonably used to re-identify any specific individual or group of individuals.

I believe it is necessary to consider a further revision to the definition of Personal information (Question 13). First, the definition of Personal Information in 2013 revised COPPA Rule does not take a unified identifier of the devices into consideration. Sequences of data collected, such as the MAC addresses or IP addresses can tell the comparable physical presence of the user. When combined with other information collected from the user, it can generate a unified profile of the child or children using the device, which should also be regarded as personal information. Second, the behavioural data of the child using the device surfing should also be considered, which can be very identical and personal. Third, biometric data including facial and voice recognition should also be included as personal information. Forth, in an environment of peer-to-peer communication based online service, an identifier that can trace back to a certain child user either with certain behaviour or able to accept incoming information should be considered as personal information.

For the Question 24, I dont think the Commission should consider a formal exception to verifiable parental consent when an operator collects an audio file with a child's voice without prior parental consent even if the audio file is collected solely as a replacement for written words, such as to perform a search or the audio file is held for a brief time and used only for that purpose. Voiceprint recognition has already been adopted by several call centres including those of financial institutions as a technology to identify the clients. Being a biometric identifier, there is a potential risk that processing such data might be misused. Even the storage of data can be attacked or hacked.

Dear Chairman Simons,

I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. 

For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I, and the patients and communities we serve with dedication, have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation at the heart of my practice and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. 

I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. 

Rachelle Lin, O.D.
The attached comments are filed on behalf of the Contact Lens Institute.

Requiring a signature from patients, even in these modified ways still creates an atmosphere of distrust and implication of dishonesty. Why would I need to get the signature of my patient to confirm they received a prescription unless I was doing something wrong that required the proof. We are required to give glasses prescriptions every time we refract a patient and generate a prescription but don't get a signed verification. In the hospital I work we have a pharmacy and sell medications but I don't get a signed verification I gave the patient a written script so they could get their medications at the pharmacy of their choice. The fact is we are caring for our patients and are expected to act in a professional and ethical manner. 

Second, the process is a burden on those using an electronic record. Having a signature pad in every exam room for patients to sign they received a prescription so it can be verified or having a patient sign a duplicate copy of their script then scan it back into the EMR, creates a burden, not only a financial burden but one of time. 

The amount of patients ordering their own contacts has steadily grown over the past number of years and with the advertising seen for online contact sales, both online and on TV I just don't see how there is such a large problem requiring a signature from every contact lens patient. We are creating more of a problem with these new rules. If the issue is patients truly not understanding they have the right to obtain a prescription for contacts, allow that language to be spelled out in the entry forms a patient signs when they check in. Require signage in the exam room or waiting room etc. There are other ways of tackling this issue besides getting in the way of the doctor patient relationship by implying their doctor is doing something wrong requiring the patient to verify a prescription was given.

The proposed regulations are overly burdensome on providers. With all the requirements relating to MIPS/PQRS, Electronic Medical Record standards being nonsensical, and the steady vertical integration and monopolization of vision insurance companies, we're already being stretched thin and pulled in all directions. Adding more paperwork and scanning work - and making it required on everyone - doesn't sound like it would be a big deal, but to a small practice it's huge.

Don't make things even harder on providers than they already are. Go start regulating 'disruptors' and online sellers and make them play by the same rules the rest of us do. It's crazy right now.
