It is repetitive and offers no value added to the patient. The FTC would do more good for the consumer if they strengthen the rule to prioritize a crackdown on internet retailers violating patient health and safety laws. We see many patients receiving incorrect or out-dated prescriptions from online sellers who simply want to make a sale regardless of accuracy.

I would like to express my concerns about the proposed Contact Lens Rule. My partners and I own 9 eye care offices in mid north Indiana. The current proposed CL rule will be another mandate which will take away patient care time and turn it into paperwork administration. Our staff takes great pride in the care we give to our patients this is a government mandated interference in the way we care for them. Not only will this require we hand the patient their prescription (which we already do...) but now we must ask them to read and sign a document that says we just gave them a copy of the prescription,plus we must now store the document for three years? This is an addition burden with no benefit to anyone.

As a practicing Optometrist for the past 22 years, I am deeply concerned about this legislation. I have personally handed contact lens prescriptions to my patients at the end of my exam for 2 decades. I point out the contact lens prescription and the expiration date to the patient so they know they have it. It is the law that I present them with the prescription and it is ethical and right. They are free to purchase their contact lenses anywhere they chose to, and have always been. I also write the expiration date on my prescriptions for 2 years, because that is the law in the state I practice in (Utah). I personally don't agree with 2 year expiration dates, but that is the law, and I obey the law. There is no restriction of patient choice in my practice, and quite honestly I don't know of any colleague of mine who does not comply with the existing law. My experience has been that many online retailers don't obey the law. The online retailer referenced in this legislation is the worst. Many prescriptions are filled after expiration dates. At times contacts are dispensed that don't match a valid prescription. I find it flabbergasting that so much credence is given to the voice of a company that is clearly only motivated by profit. The health care provider has a relationship that would be jeopardized if he or she were to deny the patient access to their legal rights to a prescription. Why would a patient ever return to such a practitioner, and yet our voice is presented as one driven by profits and self interest. It is ironic to the ultimate degree that the voice of online retailers whose sole motivation is profit, who have no interest in the individual patient, is seen as the voice representing the patients best interest. This legislation adds so much work and cost to an overburdened health care system, without benefiting patients. There are already laws that direct the patient-provider relationship. I already have more patients wanting to be examined in my practice than I have time to see. This burdensome legislation would slow down the delivery of health care in my office, and waste valuable time that now utilized to provide vision improving and saving care. Our current Lens.com customers are being put through the wringer by bad actors who simply wont release their prescriptions or provide copies of their prescription to their designated agents. Our ability at Lens.com to grow our business and attract new customers by providing more choice and competition in the marketplace is being severely hampered by the fact that patients cant get a copy of their own prescription after an eye exam.

As you correctly point out in your NRPM and in the new amendments proposed in the SNPRM, the status quo is unacceptable. The FTC needs the ability to enforce the FCLCA and crack down on bad actors who are deliberately violating the law. The FTC clearly needs more tools to help protect consumers and increase competition. We believe you have struck the correct balance with the requirement that patients proactively acknowledge they have been given a copy of their prescription and prescribers keep the record of this acknowledgment on file for three years.

Lens.com has consistently supported the idea that optometrists must demonstrate that they have provided patients with their prescriptions once they have completed their exam. This is because many optometrists do not provide patients with prescriptions despite being required to by law. We know the reason for this is because optometry offices actually make the majority of their revenue from selling contact lenses and glasses, not providing eye care services.

In the SPRM, you raise the idea of providers giving patients digital copies of their prescription as a way to acknowledge and demonstrate that they have complied with the FCLCA. As an online provider of contact lenses and an early adopter of consumer-friendly contact lens technology, we very much appreciate your desire to make it easier for customers to receive their prescriptions in a manner that allows them to easily share it with the seller of their choice. We also appreciate your desire to ensure prescribers dont skirt the law and instead give other sellers what is needed to ensure customers get the product that they want through the seller of their choice. Therefore, we support the general idea of digital copies of prescriptions. And while we support the general idea of digital copies, the operative word is copy. This is not and either/or proposition but rather, both: a digital copy may be retailed by the office and provided for the convenient retrieval by the patient after a written prescription has been provided, per the original draft of the FCLCA.

However, we believe that the devil will be in the details and that the FTC must provide more clarity and stronger protections around what constitutes a digital copy and a portal and what constitutes electronic delivery. Prescriptions are the property of patients, and shouldnt be trapped in some confusing portal of the prescribers making. The FTC needs to outline guidelines to ensure that customers can access their prescriptions via these portals with minimal hassle immediately after leaving the doctors office.

As we have pointed out in each of our earlier comment letters to the FTC around the Contact Lens Rule, the current system is rigged against consumers and companies who compete with prescribers, because unlike anyone else in the medical profession, contact lens prescribers still have the right to both prescribe and sell contact lenses at the same time and to determine what brand customers must wear. They simply have no motivation to build systems that allow their patients to take their prescriptions and shop elsewhere and have worked to erect barriers to delay, slow and do end runs around educating consumers about their rights and following the FCLCA which requires automatic prescription release.

The FTC must be vigilant about ensuring that any process or system for the digital release of a prescription is easy, accessible and follows the letter and spirit of the FCLCA. We hope your final rule takes these concerns into account.

In addition to your commitment to patient acknowledgment in the SPRM, Lens.com also supports the provisions in the SPRM which call for patients to be guaranteed the right to additional copies of their prescription. We believe that for too long the burden has been unfairly placed on consumers to have to fight for what is theirs - their prescription - and to have to go out of their way to get something which is their property and they have paid for. In some ways, it is very sad and disappointing that the FTC has had to actually make this part of the law and spell it out because providers havent been keeping up their side of the bargain that was the FCLCA.

The most important thing that the FTC can do is to wrap up the SPRM and swiftly finalize You have weighed the evidence, gone out of your way to address concerns, and written a strong rule. Lens.com is grateful, and our millions of customers will benefit as a result. 

Please move with all haste to enact the rule as drafted.

Dear Chairman Simons,

I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care in our local community. 

For more than two years, my fellow eye doctors and I, and the patients and communities we serve with dedication, have faced the threat of a seriously flawed Federal Trade Commission (FTC) plan to impose massive new costs and far-reaching new requirements on all contact lens prescribing. The proposal, even in its latest form, will divert precious resources away from the care and innovation at the heart of my practice and cast public doubt on the integrity of optometrists and ophthalmologists, our para-professional staff and other employees. It should be withdrawn once again, and re-worked to put the interests of patients, doctors, and public health and safety first. 

Its especially notable that the FTCs actions remain at odds with the policy direction being pursued by Congress and Federal agencies to prioritize the elimination of burdensome, costly and unjustified mandates in health care, especially those that are overwhelming small and mid-sized health practices on the frontlines of care. Here are active examples that I hope the agency is aware of: 

-Merit Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Special Considerations for Small Practices: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) developed the framework for MIPS acknowledging the regulatory burden that health care providers already are facing. Considering that reality, CMS reduced the number of clinicians that are required to participate. CMS supported this effort out of the agencys desire to give physicians more time with their patients, not computers. Additionally, CMS is mindful of the unique challenges that face smaller physician practices and added new bonus points for clinicians caring for patients in those settings. 

-Patients over Paperwork: CMS initiated this regulatory review in 2017 aimed at removing regulatory obstacles that get in the way of providers spending time with patients.

-Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA): Currently, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is considering eliminating or modifying the requirement for covered health care providers to make a good faith effort to obtain individuals written acknowledgment of receipt of providers Notice of Privacy Practices. The stated aim of this potential change is to reduce burden and free up resources for covered entities to devote to coordinated care. 

More than 100 U.S. Senators and House members weighed-in against the FTCs original proposal. And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country.

As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under your agencys threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions, including through the meetings we have been seeking with you and your fellow commissioners. 

Michael Murphy, O.D.

Alcon Vision, LLC, the largest eye care medical device manufacturer in the world and one of the four major manufacturers of contact lenses in the US, appreciates the opportunity to comment on the FTCs Notice of Proposed Rulemaking for the Contact Lens Rule. Alcons mission is to enhance quality of life through innovative products, increase access to quality eye care, as well as drive training and education of eye care professionals (ECPs) with the goal of improving sight around the world. Above all, Alcon is dedicated to promoting and safeguarding the eye health of all patients who benefit from our products. 
We acknowledge the Commissions objective to update the Contact Lens Rule to address current marketplace practices. Alcon believes an appropriate balance should be achieved that addresses patient safety, consumer choice and industry competition. We offer discrete comments in three areas: lens substitution, passive verification, and prescription release. 
Lens Substitution (SNPRM, p17 IIB): Alcon strongly advocates for measures that protect the clinical decision-making of ECPs when prescribing lenses, and limit manufacture and/or brand substitution. As highlighted in our April 6, 2018 comments because of differences in contact lens polymers, manufacturing techniques, lens design, optical properties, lens packaging solutions and other variables, not all contact lenses fit the same and therefore are not interchangeable. In addition, some manufactures utilize older lens materials that do not transmit as much oxygen to the eye, which can put patients eye health at risk.(1) Finally, clinical experience demonstrates the power profile (optical power of the contact lens that affects correction of vision) varies by brand, eg, all -3.00 D or +3.00 D lenses (or other power) are not the same. As a result, it is not uncommon for a patient to need one power for a given lens brand and a different power for another this can even occur with two brands from the same manufacturer. Eliminating the ability of a patient to modify the prescription as written by an ECP would ensure proper contact lens fit, optimal visual acuity, lens comfort, and ocular health. Therefore, we suggest the Commission modify the proposal allowing patients to request an alternative contact lens (eg, manufacturer/material), and have patients and sellers always adhere to the prescription written by the ECP. 
Passive Verification (SNPRM, p17 IIB): The Commissions proposal with respect to prescription verification by telephone fails to adequately address the health and safety risks associated with robocalls; calls (intentional or not) that often undermines the goal of clear and effective communication of the prescription. A verification process that includes a detailed, standardized script, eg, specific terms, requested information, presentation order, and minimum/maximum time limitations of the call, could further accomplish the shared goal of ensuring the verification of a legitimate contact lens prescription. 
Prescription Release (SNPRM, p15 IIA): Alcon continues to support any effort to improve patient access to their prescription via electronic delivery. We also believe consumers should be able to choose where to purchase their contact lenses. Subsequently, Alcon contact lenses are available for sale by ECPs and at eye care retailers, pharmacies, as well as through mail order and online retailers. 
Alcon supports the Commissions intent to minimize (or preferably eliminate) the administrative burden placed on the contact lens prescribing ECP. However, in the supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking, the Commission seeks to exempt ECPs who do not have a financial interest in the sale of contact lenses, e.g., those who work in eye care retail locations, from the requirement to obtain a patient prescription acknowledgement. Given the multitude of business relationships, it may be difficult to ascertain when an ECP may or may not have a financial interest in the sale of contact lenses. As a result, to the extent the patient acknowledgment rule is adopted, the rule should be applied to all ECPs regardless of financial interest and whether it is the ECP selling the contact lenses, or the next-door retailer or other seller. 
In summary, Alcon supports changes to the Contact Lens Rule that balance patient health and safety while at the same time preserving and protecting consumer choice in the evolving US contact lens marketplace. We appreciate the Commissions approach to provide additional clarity that will advance the benchmarks established in the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act and the goals established by the Commission. 
Thank you for consideration of our comments. 
Sincerely,
R.E. Weisbarth OD, FAAO, Vice President, Professional AffairsUS Vision Care, Alcon
Source: 1. Musgrave CSA, Fang F. Contact Lens Materials: A Materials Science Perspective. Materials (Basel). 2019;12(2):261. Published 2019 Jan 14. doi:10.3390/ma12020261.

I am a doctor of optometry providing primary eye health and vision care at a charitable clinic in Texas. I agree that it is important that consumers be given a genuine opportunity to exercise choice in the contact lens market. However, before one considers offering support for far reaching government regulations to be imposed on small businesses, its important to know the true state of the contact lens market as the market has changed tremendously since the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act was passed.

o Lens prices are competitive: The American Optometric Association (AOA) conducted a price comparison analysis in which they compared online retailer cost vs the average in-office cost to determine the dollar price difference and percent change in price for 81 different contact lenses. Of the 81 lenses studied, 28 were more expensive online, while 53 were more expensive in the doctors office. Across all lenses included in the AOAs price comparison analysis, there was an average price difference of just $0.32
o Patients Have More Retailer Options than Ever: The fastest growing distribution channel for contact lens sales in the USA was the online / Internet channel. In 2017, online retailers generated $786 million in salesgrowing by 4.9% during the 12 month ending period Dec17 and growing by 11.1% over the 24 monthending period Dec17.
o There is Widespread Agreement that the Current Rule is Working: The CEO of 1-800-CONTACTS itself acknowledged that the current rule is working in your March 2018 workshop noting, The FCLCA and CLR have succeeded in encouraging greater competition and choice in the contact lens marketplace. Consumers today have more choice and more convenience. The competitive benefits have gone beyond price. I think that the FTC can consider this a successful rule.

Doctors of optometry are concerned with your organization's claims regarding non-compliance of prescription release requirements. Despite disagreeing with the accusation regarding compliance, the profession has offered an alternative to the signed acknowledgement proposal. The proposal supported by optometry would require all contact lens prescribers to post signage in their offices notifying patients of their right to their contact lens prescription. This is a less burdensome and less intrusive approach than the current FTC proposal. This approach would also do more to broadly educate consumers. 

I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law. 

As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under FTCs threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions at both the state and federal levels.

Thank you,
Jenny Terrell, OD, FAAO, DiplABO

I am about to tell you something that you likely have NOT yet heard:
I am a Board Certified Ophthalmologist, a Fellow of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, a Fellow of the New York Academy of Medicine and a Fellow of the American College of Surgeons.
I FIT AND DISPENSE only specialty contact lenses. I do not delegate the fitting process (which is a truly on-going process) to anyone. 
The vast majority of my contact lens patients have tried contact lenses elsewhere and have not been successful at being fitted with lenses, which achieve best-corrected visual acuities, satisfactory comfort and ophthalmic SAFETY. 
I do NOT fit ANY disposable contact lenses.
Contact lenses are PROSTHESES, which sit upon our most sensitive and vital sense organs.
Unfortunately, contact have become treated as commodity items, fitted by non-physicians, and obtainable by phone, internet, pharmacies, or mail-order.
This has occurred for many reasons:
1) The contact lens manufacturing industry has trivialized the PROSTHETIC nature of contact lenses. In its efforts to capture the profits from the contact lens solutions market, they prefer patients to pay their contact lens dollars for disposable mass-produced plastic, rather than for fluids. This is solely an economic issue.
2) In the interest of giving patients "what they want", rather than what is safe, eyecare providers (many are non-M.D.'s, i.e., optometrists and dispensing opticians) have jumped on the bandwagon. This also in solely an economic issue.
3) The Government, in its quest to assist consumers in saving money, has ignored SAFETY concerns, in efforts to enable patients to obtain contact lenses from non-professional sources, to the point that after the fitting process, the clinician no longer has the ability to monitor, or to modify the contact lenses. This is also solely an economic issue.
NOT ONE of these reasons is based on patient HEALTH, or SAFETY.
Once the patient has the ability to obtain contact lenses from a multitude of sources, they often make uninformed choices in the interest of cost.
In my practice, ALMOST ALL infectious keratitis cases (corneal ulcers, infected corneal abrasions) are caused by DISPOSABLE contact lenses (not obtained from me) and foolish wear choices (i.e. continuing to wear a commoditized contact lens on an inflamed eye), which are COMPLETELY AVOIDABLE.
When, several years ago, New York State enacted a mandate to provide consumers with their contact lens "prescriptions", my fellow ophthalmologists and I were inundated with unreasonable requests from patients for contact lens prescriptions, for which they were NEVER FITTED!
I spent weeks negotiating with the NYS Attorney General to develop a form to comply with NYS law, yet not to leave me with unlimited liability, should the patient get him/herself into trouble, in the act of using their data in unwise, or dangerous ways.
I argued successfully that a "prescription" (from the Latin order, "MAKETH THOU") is literally an ORDER FROM the clinician for a pharmacist, or device dispenser to make, or to give something to the patient.
The NYS law forcing clinicians to provide contact lens DATA, is truly NOT A PRESCRIPTION, since the request almost never comes from the clinician, but from the PATIENT, under GOVERNMENT mandate.
The NYS Attorney General agreed, and permitted me to use the language "contact lens DATA", and further permitted me to include the statement, "these DATA do not constitute a PRESCRIPTION", since the request for same originated with the patient, and NOT the clinician. He agreed that should the patient incur injury, for having used these data improperly, that this statement would shield me from liability, for being forced to do something that I consider CLINICALLY UNWISE. 
In addition he permitted me to release the requested contact lens data (like any other part of the medical record) with only a written, signed request. 
There was NO mandate for requiring the patient to acknowledge RECEIPT IN WRITING, other than keeping a copy of the data form in the patients chart. 
It is hard enough to get patients to sign the myriad of already government-mandated forms. 
In addition, my experience has demonstrated that most patients, who request contact lens data, do not want to travel to the office for the data and only want the data mailed to them. 
Once requested, I have found that these patient RARELY EVER return to my office, initially saying that they just want the data "for travel purposes", resulting in un-ending, un-supervised contact lens dispensing and use, from then on.
I truly hope that the FTC will put patient SAFETY ahead of FINANCIAL considerations.
The FTC's mandating that patients have the right to inflict injury upon themselves, without the medical knowledge to make such a decision, is immoral.
Do NOT enact such an FTC mandate!
The eyes of America are precious to both patients (who usually don't realize it until injured) and to clinicians, who care for them.

I strongly urge the FTC to withdraw its latest proposed changes to the Contact Lens Rule and focus on efforts to enhance patient safety. Thank you for your consideration.

Dear FTC Commissioners and Staff,

Below please find a statement from the National Hispanic Medical Association and the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) in response to the Federal Trade Commissions (FTC) request for comments on its Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on the Contact Lens Rule (16 CFR Part 315, Project No. R511995). We want to thank the FTC staff for all the time and attention they have put in over the past years to craft a final Contact Lens Rule that will help millions of Americans, especially Hispanics and other underserved populations, understand their rights as contact lens consumers, to have access to their own contact lens prescriptions and be afforded more choice, more competition and more access in the marketplace. 

LULAC & NHMA STRONGLY SUPPORT THE FTCS PROPOSED CONTACT RULE 

As we have stated throughout this process and in our comments around the original NPRM and the Workshop, the Federal Trade Commissions proposed amendments to the Contact Lens Rule are an important victory for Hispanic working families who rely on the convenience, choice and savings that comes from being able to take your prescription for contact lenses and shop where you want, when you want. Every day, more and more Hispanics enter the market for contact lenses. We are the fastest growing demographic but our families simply do not know their rights as consumers, especially our right to a copy of prescription and this is critical because you cant buy contact lenses without a prescription.

The system here in the US for buying contact lenses is stacked against consumers because the people who issue you your prescription are also allowed to sell you contact lenses at the very same time. Consumers who dont know their rights are getting trapped in the exam chair so to speak, unaware that they can buy lenses elsewhere for lower prices.

Consumers can buy contact lenses online, at the drugstore or when they are doing their weekly shopping at Costco, comparing prices and getting the best deal for their families. We are not opposed to Hispanic consumers buying their contact lenses from their eye doctors but they should have a choice and a copy of their own prescription.

RESPONDING TO THE QUESTIONS IN THE 5-28 SNPRM ON THE CONTACT LENS RULE

PRESCRIPTION RELEASE ACKNOWLEDGMENT IS ESSENTIAL TO ENSURE THAT HISPANIC CONSUMERS KNOW THEIR RIGHT TO THEIR CONTACT LENS PRESCRIPTION

When the proposed new Contact Lens Rule was first introduced, LULAC and NHMA applauded the addition of a requirement for optometrists to obtain a signed acknowledgement after providing a prescription to a consumer, and to keep that acknowledgement on file for three years. A signed acknowledgment gives the FTC a means to track those who are failing to follow the prescription release requirement under FCLCA and to take action on behalf of consumers' rights when a case warrants.

We understand that the optometrists and their allies have since raised questions about the burdens that they claim could result from adding a signed acknowledgment form to the exam and contact lens fitting process. We do not share their concerns. Our community continually has been victimized and denied their prescriptions by prescribers and doctors at a higher rate than most other Americans. We strongly believe that more must be done to ensure patients are informed of their rights and given copies of their prescription, as many copies as they need and ask for. 

This focus on burdens that providers might face is upsetting when one remembers just how many patients are being robbed of their right to lower prices and more convenient shopping and being denied a copy of something that they worked hard to pay for, namely their own prescription.

USING TECHNOLOGY TO ENSURE HISPANIC CONTACT LENS CONSUMERS KNOW THEIR RIGHTS AND CAN ACCESS THEIR PRESCRIPTION IS A GOOD IDEA AS LONG AS IT IS DESIGNED FAIRLY AND IS EASY TO USE

The question of prescribers and sellers creating portals for customers in order to share prescription information is a little more of a complex question and may in fact create a greater burden initially on doctors and their patients. There is no doubt that more and more families and medical practices are storing critical health and wellness information in secure clouds and portals. 

In conclusion, the most important point we can stress to the FTC is the critical and time sensitive need to finalize and start enforcing the Contact Lens Rule as soon as possible. We urge you to swiftly issue the final Contact Lens Rule.

Sincerely,

Dr Elena Rios, President & CEO of the National Hispanic Medical Association
Sindy Benavides, Chief Executive Officer of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC)

Patients Have More Retailer Options than Ever: The fastest growing distribution channel for contact lens sales in the USA was the online / Internet channel. In 2017, online retailers generated $786 million in salesgrowing by 4.9% during the 12 month ending period Dec17 and growing by 11.1% over the 24 monthending period Dec17.
There is Widespread Agreement that the Current Rule is Working:The CEO of 1-800-CONTACTS itself acknowledged that the current rule is working in a March 2018 FTC workshop noting, The FCLCA and CLR have succeeded in encouraging greater competition and choice in the contact lens marketplace. Consumers today have more choice and more convenience. The competitive benefits have gone beyond price. I think that the FTC can consider this a successful rule.

Doctors of optometry are concerned with the FTCs claims regarding non-compliance of prescription release requirements. Despite disagreeing with the accusation regarding compliance, the profession has offered an alternative to the signed acknowledgement proposal put forward by the Commission. The proposal supported by optometry would require all contact lens prescribers to post signage in their offices notifying patients of their right to their contact lens prescription. This is a less burdensome and less intrusive approach than the proposal put forward by the FTC. This approach would also do more to broadly educate consumers.

I have and will continue to comply fully with the prescription release requirements of the 2003 Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. The agencys own records and data clearly demonstrate that eye doctors across the country, in overwhelming numbers, comply as well. Instead of creating new burdens from Washington, DC impacting tens of thousands of doctors and millions of patients, please commit to a program of basic enforcement focused on outliers shown to be violating the law.

In all, through letters, direct exchanges during committee hearings and committee report language, more than 100 Members of Congress Republicans and Democrats -- have spoken out against the FTCs misguided approach to updating the contact lens rule and called on the agency to prioritize a crackdown on illegal device sales, including those being reported on by the national media --https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/21/business/media/hubble-contact-lens.html.And now, since the May 2019 release of the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rule Making, more than 25 U.S. Senators have registered their continued concern with the Commissions proposed new requirements, stating that the FTCs reaffirmation of a prescription release confirmation proposal is both unnecessary and overly burdensome. According to the FTCs own data, few complaints regarding prescription release have been received and the Commission estimates that this new mandate would add millions in new regulatory compliance costs. It is especially troubling that the Commissions stated intent is to gain new investigative authority to target small and mid-sized independent medical practices serving communities in our state and across the country.

As I understand it, the purpose of the ten-year review of the Contact Lens Rule is to assess its effectiveness based on a thorough, fact-based analysis and a process free of bias, false claims and insider-influenced policy. Doctors, like me, and our patients across the United States who are continuing to live and work under FTCs threat of baseless and punishing regulations look forward to participating in open and thoughtful discussions at both the state and federal levels.

Sincerely,

Priya Patel, O.D.

As the medical director of a hospitalist program at the intersection of rural Tennessee and Virginia, I have a unique perspective on the devastation caused by the opioid and addiction crises in this country, as well as the obstacles to effective solutions. While the resulting devastation of lives, families and businesses knows no socioeconomic or geographic boundaries, there are disproportionate barriers that people in rural communities face when it comes to addiction treatment. Ballad Health is partnering with East Tennessee State University (ETSU), Milligan College, Emory & Henry College and other community partners to remove these barriers.
After last years merger between Wellmont and Mountain States, ETSU was able to partner with Ballad Health to create a new fellowship program in addiction medicine. Hospitals are uniquely positioned to play a critical role in stemming the tide of opioid addiction, but the effort requires more highly trained and certified providers available at these reachable moments in the care path. As part of its commitment to expand education and training in the region, the newly-merged Ballad Health is set to fund any un-reimbursed costs of this fellowship program, which over a 10-year period could top more than $2.5 million. 
In May of this year, Milligan College announced its own partnership with Ballad Health to create a training program in addictions counseling, helping to round out education for the continuum of care in addiction treatment by adding a pipeline of counseling professionals to complement the medical professionals coming through the ETSU program. 
Ballad Health is also working to strengthen the pipeline of medical professionals who can help extend the reach of physician in primary care and other settings. I have personally participated in training for physician assistants through the Emory & Henry College School of Health Sciences, and their students perform rotations in our Virginia facilities. 
In addition to these training programs, of note is Ballad Healths $85 million investment commitment in behavioral health, which is helping to strengthen addiction recovery services and community partnerships like Overmountain Recovery. In a region that is among both the top 10 nationally for opioid abuse AND second in the nation for rural hospital closures over the past decade, these types of investments are urgent. The fact that those investments are being made is cause for optimism. 
Nothing short of innovative and locally-focused public, private and academic partnerships will be able to halt the trajectory of this regions addiction crisis. The programs at ETSU and Milligan College would not have gotten off the ground without the commitment and combined resources from Ballad Health, of which I remain a strong supporter. 
Regards, 
Shyam Odeti, MD, MS, FAAFP, FHM.

As a physician with 19 years of experience caring for patients in the Northeast Tennessee / Southwest Virginia region, I supported the merger when it was proposed, and I remain supportive today. The merger of Mountain States Health Alliance and Wellmont Health System to become Ballad Health has created new opportunities for healthcare providers to not just treat the sick, but to reach upstream of acute encounters to address the root causes of the health issues that disproportionately affect our region, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity and cardiovascular disease. 

Prior to the merger, both health systems had the desire to address these issues but neither had the resources. Now, instead of putting our limited resources into unnecessary duplication, were able to shift our focus toward population health improvement. This means building a structure and a long-term plan for addressing the specific health problems that plague our region. By reinvesting the efficiencies obtained through integrating the two health systems, Ballad Health has committed to invest more than $300 million over 10 years in improving the health of our region, including $28 million specifically toward rural health services. Weve already partnered to launch an Accountable Care Community to address regional health needs with participation from more than 220 regional organizations. Ballad Health has also partnered with East Tennessee State University to help create the Center for Rural Health Research to identify new mechanisms to improve health in rural and nonurban communities.

These are major steps forward that will truly make a difference in the lives of people in our region for generations to come. As an emergency physician, Ive seen the problems first hand. Now Im excited to be part of a comprehensive solution that has the potential to transform the health of our region. None of this would be possible without the creation of Ballad Health.

To Whom It May Concern:

Many physicians, including myself, pursued this career because we love helping people and want to make a difference. We hate feeling like we are too late to have the kind of impact our patients really need. 

But here in Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia, we face that feeling all too often. As a primary care physician who serves in both a Ballad Health Medical Associates practice and as the medical director of Providence Medical Clinic, which provides free healthcare to people in need, I do everything I can to set people on a course for better health. 

Unfortunately, I cannot undo decades of poor lifestyle choices with their diets, activity levels, and addictions. As a result, many of my patients, especially those at Providence Medical Clinic, dont just suffer from a single illness or ailment. They have chronic, major issues such as behavioral health conditions, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity and lung disease from tobacco use. 

With the formation of Ballad, we are now able to focus more of our efforts on issues of health which are plaguing our region in order to make a lasting impact on our patients. With our renewed focus on population health issues in our region, true culture change is more likely to occur. 

In the 18 months since Ballad Healths launch, our medical care is regularly recognized among the top of our region and nation, and we have done tremendous work in improving access to primary care, hospital services and specialist medicine. 

Ballad Health was also among the first 30 organizations in the nation and the only one spanning two states to create an Accountable Care Community, a collaborative group that consists of more than 200 individual organizations with more than 250 representatives who have joined forces to improve community health, knowing to do so involves efforts aimed at educational success and economic opportunity. 

The ACC aligns efforts from all sectors of our communities and region. Working together, we are focused on addressing the upstream causes of chronic disease and other health problems. 

Those causes are not always immediately apparent, but we do know exposure to Adverse Childhood Experiences, also known as social traumas, increases the risk for alcohol and drug abuse, depression, smoking and suicide, all of which are obvious health concerns. They also raise the chances for unsafe sexual practices, poor work and academic performance, domestic and sexual violence and financial stress, which can also have negative impacts on health. 

Many of our regions health issues can be traced to multi-generational struggles with these issues. The goal of the ACC, then, as well as so many of Ballad Healths programs and initiatives, is to reduce these high-risk health behaviors before they have a chance to damage our next generations health and well-being. 

Beyond that, we have resolved to do something just as vital: to listen. After all, if Ballad Health is to be a strong advocate in addressing the tough problems our region faces, we need to put additional effort into listening to our population about what they have experienced and what they need.

The world is full of suffering, but it is also full of overcoming. That is why I support Ballad Healths initiatives and efforts because through the work we are doing together, we can help our region overcome so much. 

Sincerely,

Marta J Wayt, DO, FACP

I am a physician who came to the region roughly ten years ago, and am not employed by Ballad.
 
My tenure in the region has afforded me the opportunity to witness the changes the merger has brought to our healthcare. Holston Valley, the flagship hospital of Wellmont was consistently losing money year after year. It was a victim of the redundant services Wellmont believed it needed to offer in order to compete with Mountain States. For example, two Level I trauma centers and two NICUs in a region of this size did not make economic sense nor did it improve care. Two hospitals within a few miles of each other, Indian Path (Mountain States) and Holston Valley (Wellmont), also duplicated services as the systems competed to attract patients. Competition is good! It lowers costs to consumers, and improves quality. Except in this sort of situation. Both systems were spending (wasting) resources to compete with the other, duplicating high revenue services, while neglecting other services needed in the community; mental health and addiction medicine. There simply wasnt enough money to compete and have resources left to fill those needs. Enter, the COPA.
 
With the merging of the systems, under the close supervision of the TN and VA Departments of Health, the foolish waste of money spent duplicating services could be eliminated while improving the actual quality and available services to the community. No longer would there be a need to have two level one trauma centers, or two NICUs when one would concentrate the skilled personnel required to run such programs, effectively improving care and reducing costs. With the commitments made under the COPA, the resultant savings would not serve to pad the Health Systems bottom line, but instead be reinvested in the community, adding the much needed services mentioned above and ensuring solvency into the future, rather than risking an unserviceable debt burden that could threaten the existence of lower producing hospitals, like those in the rural parts of the region.
 
Is it working? Since the merger the system has been able to consolidate services, improving efficiency and reducing costs, while improving quality in almost every metric. Still in its infancy, Ballad is already delivering on the promises it made to the community; with the improvement of quality mentioned above, recruitment of new physicians to the area, maintenance of rural hospitals, and development of mental health services. The region is finally on track to improve care at all its hospitals, and reduce wasteful spending at the same time.
 
Despite the initial successes, the challenges put upon the new health system has resulted in anger by some who believe healthcare in the region is deteriorating. A nursing shortage affecting many cities (not just here) has negatively impacted the efficiency of our emergency departments and reduced our effective capacity. As a patient it would be easy, and understandable, to attribute this change to the merger, when in reality, the merger has made it possible to increase nursing salaries, and improve retention and recruiting efforts. Another change is that the citizens of Kingsport no longer have a Level I Trauma Center or NICU, and now must drive 20-30 minutes to Johnson City. As a result some of them believe Ballad and the COPA is failing them, and it is understandable that they feel this way; they are experiencing what they perceive is a decrease in available services. The reality paints a different picture, however. One important aspect of the change is that by consolidating care in one hospital, the quality can improve. Our region simply does not have the population to support the number of specialized physicians required to maintain two high-quality Level I centers and NICUs. This is evident in the squandered resources prior to the merger and missed quality measures prior to the consolidation.
 
As a physician, husband, father, and occasional patient, I am confident in the decision made by our Department of Health to allow the merger between Wellmont and Mountain States. Reduced cost, improved quality and access and new services are already in progress. I believe, through adherence to the COPA, care will continue to improve, and citizens of our unique region will benefit for years to come. I also believe that those who are rightfully concerned will come to appreciate the advantages the merger brings to region; quality, access, and sustainability.

Loot Boxes, as well as microtransactions in general, have caused game companies to become too greedy for their own good through psychologically manipulating people both kids and adults into spending exorbitant amounts of money on goods that should not have been for purchased in the first place in a full-price $60 game. FIFA (EA) Ultimate Team, in which players can create their own soccer teams, utilize loot boxes in order to trick people into spending more money than the initial price. Additionally, FIFA, Madden, and NHL are rated "E" for everyone, meaning that parents who are not aware of these predatory practices are especially vulnerable and these companies even add microtransactions and loot boxes AFTER the game releases and get good reviews in order to avoid bad press. Companies such as Electronic Arts (EA), Activision (Publisher of Call of Duty), Take-Two Interactive (publisher of Grand Theft Auto), and Ubisoft (publisher of Assassin's Creed) are the most prominent mainstream Tripple-A (meaning the budget being used to make the games) that use these tactics to milk those who are vulnerable and or don't know any better into spending even more money. These practices originated from the mobile game industry. 

Mobile games are especially predatory, as they provide various predatory manipulation in order for the player to PROGRESS in the game by paying money in order to complete your objectives in-game. These games are not made to be enjoyed by consumers, they are meant to be slot machines first and video games second. The mobile market and the mainstream video game market go after "whales", those people who are psychologically manipulated by microtransactions and are the primary target for these practices, the 1%. This small percentage of people are those who suffer from gambling and shopping addictions, as well as those who have not been exposed yet but are a qualified target for these practices. To trick people that these mobile cell phone games are safe, they abe; them as free to play, but Now, the reason they utilize these tactics is that consumers are more cautious about purchasing when the item of interest is marked at a price point, so they mark them as free so they can be suckered into playing the game and spending more money than they would have if they just bought the game if it was marked at a price. This spending s can be anywhere from $5 to hundreds or thousands of dollars on in-app purchases in the app

As you can see, there is no reason to include these predatory practices other than to milk that small percentage of consumers for the sake of avarice for the corporate executives at the top. These people don't see us as a consumer, but rather, contrary to what their public relations department would have you believe, cattle to be exploited. Now, I should state that I don't think there is anything wrong with a publicly-traded company, but when you use tactics that prey on the vulnerable like a disease infects the human body, then you don't deserve support from anyone, and you don't deserve to be in business, period. It is unfortunate that corporate avarice had infected the gaming industry, and I wish that the ESRB would do something to self-regulate themselves, but alas, they don't see it as a problem so now we as consumers have to now plea to the US Government to safeguard our hobby and do what ESRB could not do in the first place, take action against loot boxes and hopefully microtransactions by extension.

As someone who has played video games my entire life for the past 21 years, it saddens me to see the industry fall to such a low state. They say that the reason they do these practices is to get money to cover development costs but in reality, the make more than enough money back from game sales to get a significant net-income. It just is depressing to see the industry that I love fall to lying in order to cover themselves up. This madness cannot be allowed to continue otherwise the future of the industry would devolve from artist visions to slot machines.

Loot boxes showcase the exact same signs of manipulation to gambling in brain activity, so while they don't reward you with items that can be turned into money, they still exploit your mind into buying into randomized garbage so the executives at the top can rake in more money without moral consequences or qualms. All the while they lie to our faces about needing to make more money to cover development costs, which, even if it was true, would still be incredibly disheartening. I care for video games, almost as much as I care for my own parents even, so I only wish that the industry as a whole can realize the mistakes they have made before it is too late. It is with all of these things in mind that I ask you to do what the industry themselves refused to do, and regulate Loot boxes please, or better yet, ban them. These practices are vile and predatory in nature and if we give them an inch, they will take a mile.

That same fierce determination to go above and beyond in the service of others extends to our doctors and nurses, who have been proudly serving not just their communities, but the communities of southwest Virginia, southeast Kentucky, and northwest North Carolina. Since 1935, Kingsport's flagship hospital, Holston Valley Community Medical Center, has been a proud bastion of hope for not just our community, but our entire region. We are a proud city that embodies the volunteer spirit of our state and the pioneer spirit of our country's founding fathers. But now that capacity to serve others is threatened by monopolistic practices that are creating a culture of fear in our hospitals and communities.

Because of the joint TN-VA COPA and the subsequent Ballad Merger, amazing doctors and nurses are leaving in droves, as they are unable to speak out against the changes incurred by Ballad under threat of termination. Countless patient horror-stories of inadequate care, excessive wait times, ridiculous billing expenses, disturbing uncleanliness, potential HIPPA violations, and life-threatening situations abound. 

Despite the fact that data from a Ballad-commissioned study by the firm Bishop & Associates of CA showed that leaving Johnson City as the only Level 1 Trauma Center in this region would exclude 84,147 people from the "Golden Hour" of trauma, Ballad is trudging ahead with their plans to downgrade Holston Valley. In comparison, 17,750 would be excluded if Holston Valley was selected as the Level 1. In addition, Kingsport is home to the headquarters of the Eastman Chemical Company (which has exploded twice, most recently in 2017), the Domtar Paper Mill, and the BAE Army Ammunition Plant (which exploded in January of this year). A major industrial catastrophe in Kingsport would be crippling if we were to suffer it without a Level 1 Trauma Center. 

Behind the scenes, a group of 15 business and community "leaders" who call themselves the "Hole-In-The-Wall-Gang" spearheaded this merger and made it happen. As a cardiologist and a lifelong resident of Northeast Tennessee, I am closely familiar with the health issues that are particular to our region. We suffer from disproportionately high rates of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, and tobacco use. Every day, I care for people who represent one or more or frequently all of these health risks. It is clear to me, and to many of my colleagues, that a greater effort is needed to intervene upstream of these issues and work to address health determinants before they result in significant comorbidities and early mortality. 

I strongly supported the Ballad Health merger in the beginning, and now that I have worked with the new health system for 18 months, I am even more convinced that this model of region-wide collaboration is the best way for us to address both the challenges that are unique to our region (such as health disparities) and those that all physicians and health systems in the United States share (such as payment reform). As separate health systems, Wellmont and Mountain States were not able to achieve the scale necessary to make the maximum impact on population health, nor were we able to fully align our efforts to participate in value based contracts in a way that would make the greatest impact. 

Since the merger, Ballad Health has formed a department of population health and an Accountable Care Community with more than 120 participating organizations, all focused on addressing the upstream causes of heart disease and other health problems. Ballad Health is working toward closer integration with the physician practices supported by the health system in rural parts of our region, creating access to specialty services like cardiology in places that previously had no such resource. Through collaboration within Ballad Health, my practice has also been able to participate in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, creating the opportunity to reduce the overall cost of care by participating in value based contracts on a scale not possible before. 

I remain a strong supporter of Ballad Health and the innovative approach to population health improvement, cost reduction and quality improvement that the system represents.

My 10 year old child was a victim of an online public information search company where my child's name and address was publically available on the web (WhitePages.com, Spokeo.com, etc.). More data on my child could be bought for a price $1 - $20. I was shocked as to how this may have happened and had to go to great lengths to have the Personally Identifiable Information removed from many similar websites. This took a lot of time and cost me in lost work hours. Many parents would not have the luxury, time, or knowledge on how to remove this data, nor should we expect them to. The Public has no time to monitor every aspect of their personal data, we expect the government to protect us from corporate abuse of our privacy.

The American Public expects that PII of a minor child could never be revealed publically online or bought for a price in the first place. How was the data available? Why could someone buy/sell more information about my child? Through a children's magazine subscription that was "sold" to a paying partner? Through school? Through a Dr's office? Through apps?

Corporations and computer programmers will cry that they "need" the data for their livelihood to "make thing better" for us but what about our privacy? The buying and selling of Personally Identifiable Information is shared with so many companies it makes it hard to know who to punish.

I think I speak for most families when I say I do not have the time or law education to fully understand this bill but to have had this experience tells me the COPPR is not working for the online privacy of children. 

Please protect our children from these companies who profit from our children's data. The European Union has very strict rules concerning children, perhaps we can learn about what is working for them in this area because it's does not working for us in the United States. We cannot expect corporations to monitor themselves considering so much money can be made by selling children's data. Thank you.

Re: Safeguard Rule, 16 CFR part 314, Project No. P145407

Dear Sir/Madam:

I am writing to comment on the above-captioned proposed amendment to the Safeguard Rule, 16 CFR part 314. The New York Insurance Association (NYIA) is the state trade association that has represented the property and casualty insurance industry in New York for more than 135 years. Our membership includes numerous insurance carriers in varying size. 

As you are aware, the New York Department of Financial Services (DFS) issued its Cybersecurity Regulation for Financial Services Companies (Regulation 500, 23 NYCRR 500, et seq.) in 2016. The final implementation date for this regulation, however, did not go into effect until March 1, 2019. While these proposed amendments to the Safeguard rule are based in part upon DFS Regulation 500, it is NYIAs view that it is premature for the Commission to adopt such rules at the federal level before sufficient data on the experience of both regulated entities and consumers with this regulation is available for public review. DFS, for example, could issue periodic changes to Regulation 500 as it gathers additional information about the efficacy of its regulation leading to inconsistencies between the Commissions rules and the cybersecurity laws and regulations in New York, the nations leading financial center. 

Furthermore, NYIA has concerns about the proposals provision that would seem to substitute the Commissions judgment over a companys governance decisions as overreaching. A company board has every reason to safeguard its personal identifying information (PII), as well as its reputation and future growth prospects which would be jeopardized by poor stewardship of PII. An additional concern is the proposals provision to include encryption for all consumer data, except where a chief security information officer (CISO) has approved of effective alternative compensating controls. This runs the risk that companies might feel compelled to encrypt all consumer data regardless of whether the CISOs compensating controls would be second guessed in the event a company were to lose unencrypted customer information. 
Another concern with the proposal is the mandate of multi-factor authentication for anyone accessing a companys internal networks that contain customer information. The proposal, were it enacted, should clarify that multi-factor authentication should only apply to access from outside the internal network. 

As always, please feel free to contact me if you have any questions or wish to discuss this matter further. Thank you for your consideration of our comments. 

Sincerely,
 
Ellen D. Melchionni, CAE
President

I'm glad to see this rule being reviewed. Having two children, it is extremely worrisome to see schools using technology in a way that children's personal information of all types can, and are collected on a regular basis. My kids MUST use google classroom in school, and turn in assignments via google. This information which is the result of teacher assignments, asking for kids to write about opinion pieces, demonstrating decision making, among other assignments can be used to develop an entire personality profile on a single child. 
I have witnessed online apps where the app simply asks the child's age, with no additional proof requirement, then proceeds to asks series of questions, again, all of which are developed to produce a data profile of the children playing. 
I believe our government, which guarantees certain rights under the 4th and 9th Amendment, has an obligation to protect our children, above all else, from unknowingly giving up their rights of all forms of privacy online, to include, IP Address & other computer identifiers. I would like to see where all biometric identifiable information becomes the property of the person to whom it belongs, and is not allowed to be used in any form as data mining information. Within the past two years or more I am witnessing more and more of our personal identifiable information being collected without proper permission. I enter the doctor's office with my children and the front desk persons are asking my children to have their palm read for the biometric identifier without even asking parental permission. They act as if it is a requirement. We enter another office and they tell us they need a facial picture to be scanned into their software for identification. My son recently called our bank about his debit card and was asked to perform a voice identifier so his voice could be used for his identification. Our family has the been the victim of identity theft on three occasions. Although we did not end up with a breach of our credit or monetary loss, it shows the risk involved with allowing our children to have their identifiable information on the web in ANY way. Some of this information (biometrics) cannot be "re-made". Once it has been breached and misused, there is no making a "new" hand, eye, face, etc. Please raise the age limit for the collection of any private data, please make ALL private data the property of the person whom entered the information, and please make a very stiff penalty if it is ever found misused. We seem to be going down a slippery slope of losing all right to privacy.

This report is being submitted in response to the FTC call for research under the workshop of Nixing the Fix in relation to withholding of parts for repair by manufacturers. The title of the report is "A Study of Gray Market Prices for Restricted Rolex Watch Parts". See attached files.

ABSTRACT 
This report presents a research study concerning pricing effects on restricted Rolex watch parts based on 2008 wholesale prices compared to that of 2019. Data is presented in spreadsheet form and demonstrates that the open market average wholesale price increased by 563% over that period compared to a 19% inflation rate. It is shown that this is a consequence of restricted parts policies of the manufacturer and is discussed in the context of a gray versus black market for goods.

There is a chance that the cost can be lower than what you would have otherwise paid if you had been given the opportunity to purchase the item directly (gambling). Keep in mind also that nobody's arguing against the free loot boxes that are handed out for free. It's specifically the loot boxes that are being sold that are the issue.

Vindictus comes out with a new character. In their shop they happen to have a bunch of outfits. However, all of the good outfits are locked behind loot boxes. Sales of loot boxes, whether directly or indirectly, via in-game currency (bought in exchange for real money) are unequivocally a form of gambling because the loot boxes: 1. Are able to be be bought with in-game currency, within or without an in-game secondary market 2. The in-game currency has a quantifiable real money value by mathematical conversion rate, and 3. The loot boxes simulate a gambling mechanism via randomized result that gives a tangible benefit and/or faster progress in the game. This also meets the legal requirements of promoting gambling (including and especially to minors) in a rapidly growing list of countries. 

Indirect sales of loot boxes are not a valid loophole to get around classification of gambling if it is still _possible_ to purchase the loot boxes using in-game currency (on a secondary market in or out of game, for example). It doesn't matter if the publisher or another player gets paid directly, what matters is that currency with a real money equivalence is being spent by the player for the loot box. Game publishers can come up with a nearly infinite array of ways to conceal purchases via indirect means. If indirect sales of loot boxes were to be a valid loophole, attempts to regulate loot boxes would never have any teeth.

While the Apple App Store has a policy regarding loot boxes: "Apps offering loot boxes or other mechanisms that provide randomized virtual items for purchase must disclose the odds of receiving each type of item to customers prior to purchase." (Apple App Store Review Guidelines, sec. 3.1.1, In-App Purchase), they do not enforce this policy. Instead they direct consumers reporting violations to address their complaints to the game publisher directly, whom of course is not going to be inclined to find fault with itself. I know this because I filed a complaint with the Google Play Store on loot boxes available for purchase within an app called Pixel Starships, and got no response at all. I then filed the same complaint directly to Apple reporting the apparent violation of Apple App Store Review Guidelines policy, and the response I got was, "Please know that while iTunes is the vendor of the app, we do not have control on what goes on within the application, the mechanics of the application, or delivery of the content. The iTunes Store simply processes the financial aspect of the transaction on behalf of the developer.". 

So I did take my concerns regarding the sale of loot boxes up with the developer of Pixel Starships, SavySoda, and this is the response I got from a developer of the game: "At the end of the day, games are designed to keep players engaged for as long as possible in anyway feasible way it can. If anything, the fact that it is used prominently in gambling games just reinforces my point. They're effective in keeping players engaged."

Pixel Starships is currently marketed by SavySoda on the Google Play Store as being appropriate for children ages 10 and up.

Loot boxes are gambling by definition because they are purchased with a wager made using in-game currency whose real money equivalent valuation can be calculated quantitatively, produce a randomized outcome, in which if you win you get a perceived advantage or faster progress in the game. Game publishers do this for the express purpose of reinforcing addictive behavior, even to the extent of bragging about how "addictive" a game is as a sign of quality. Companies selling known addictive products must be regulated as such. Loot boxes should be classified as gambling, because game developers are shameless, and are currently marketing addiction behavior training to children directly as aggressively as humanly possible.

When a consumer purchases an item from a manufacturer, that item is no longer under the control of the manufacturer whatsoever. Private property rights are a cornerstone of our economy and laws, and the right to repair our own possessions is part of the definition of owning those possessions. As the purchases available from manufacturers are more complex today than in the past, the issue arises that the original manufacturer might be the only entity capable of performing necessary repairs on their products. While this may be true, manufacturers should not intentionally use their dominance in the market to prevent other entities from offering repairs to consumers under the guise of product quality while in reality the companies are concerned about their bottom lines. Allowing companies to control how their products are repaired would create opportunities for those companies to engage in anti-competitive practices by preventing third party repair services from offering an alternative to the demands of the manufacturer. Such practices are anti-consumer and damaging to the open market. In addition, by allowing companies to control both quality assurance on their products as well as their repairs, a conflict of interest is created where a company has an incentive to sell low quality, easy to damage products because such products would bring in revenue from repairs consumers cannot get anywhere else. Products purchased by a consumer belong to them and the right to repair those products as the owner sees fit is a cornerstone of private property. Any other approach to private property sets a dangerous precedent for the open market and our values as a nation.

Safelite is not only the nations largest purchaser of Original Equipment Equivalent (OEE) replacement vehicle glass, we are also the nations largest purchaser (outside of vehicle manufacturers themselves) of Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) logoed/branded vehicle glass which we typically purchase directly from the vehicle manufacturers. So, we dont see ourselves as a competitor but a partner of the vehicle manufacturers. 

However, this partnership is becoming increasingly strained because of how vehicle manufacturers are positioning OEM vehicle glass parts and service with the advent of new Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) features such as Lane Departure Warning, Lane Keeping Assist, etc. When a vehicle with ADAS enabled by a front facing camera system has a windshield replaced, vehicle manufacturers require that a recalibration of the ADAS system be performed and it is that specific situation where vehicle manufacturers are Nixing the Fix.

Over the past eighteen months, using state of the art equipment manufactured by Bosch, Safelite has successfully performed 400,000 front camera ADAS recalibrations on vehicles representing twenty eight vehicle makes from Audi to Volvo. These recalibrations have been successfully performed on OEM and OEE windshields. We are confident this volume of experience qualifies us as not only vehicle glass repair and replacement specialists, but also ADAS recalibration specialists. In fact, as part of a multi-national company our dedicated technical innovation team exists for the sole purpose of developing the best technologies to serve our customers. Our commitment to ADAS recalibration across all vehicle makes, models and years is unmatched in the VGRR industry, investing millions of dollars in ADAS recalibration technology in the past five years. 

It is disturbing then to have our customers, who for whatever reason, make contact with a new vehicle dealer and when inquiring about ADAS recalibration, they are told in the best case your vehicle MUST have an OEM windshield or worst case you must use OEM branded glass and the car needs to be (re) calibrated at a dealer for the system to work to the most incriminatory using non-OEM glass will void your warranty. These difficult situations are a regular occurrence for Safelite to have to manage with individual vehicle owners, as well as our fleet customers. Regardless of how bold and aggressive the tactics, all such statements are purposefully intended to sow fear and doubt in the mind of the customer with the hope that the customer will feel compelled to go to the dealership to purchase OEM glass and have the dealership perform the recalibration. 

In some situations, after Safelite installed an OEE windshield, having learned of the scare tactics of the dealer and/or the vehicle manufacturer, the customer demanded OEM glass be installed. So, we unnecessarily had to remove a perfectly good piece of OEE glass, wait for the delivery of OEM glass and then reinstallall at Safelites cost. Not fair to the customer, nor Safelite or any other service provider qualified to perform ADAS recalibration services. This unfortunate but recurring problem is increasing in frequency, as most new vehicles are equipped with ADAS.

But dont take just our word for it. Exhibit D goes even further with this vehicle manufacturer stating that only their dealers can perform the recalibration servicepatently untrue, misleading and deceptive to the reader. Upon hearing or reading such scaremongering it is no surprise that an individual vehicle owner will turn away from the aftermarket and head to the new vehicle dealer to ensure that their warranty and safety not be jeopardized. 

Over the past seventy-two years, Safelite, as the nations largest vehicle glass repair, replacement and now recalibration specialist, has worked tirelessly to build trust and confidence with individual vehicle owners and fleet customers alike. Hello. 

Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments regarding to "Made in USA" claims. 

I was fooled for many years by product makers' words regarding their products being "Made in USA" or "Product of USA." One of the best examples is when the packaging states "Made in USA," but after purchasing, the truth comes out on, say, the operating instructions. Then and only then can a consumer learn the truth.....i.e., the item was not made in the United States, rather it only was distributed from the company's headquarters in the United States. 

If I remember correctly, my first experience with this was with a Ryobi electric sander at Home Depot. There, the products are displayed without boxes/instruction sheets. I believe that the description of the sander I was looking at had "Made in USA" either on the actual tool or on Home Depot's "description tag" that shows model number, etc. It was only after they brought one down from the shelf and I took it home and opened the box that I learned the real story about the sander from the instructions packed inside. Made in China. Distributed from their warehouse in the USA.

Since that time, I've been careful to either contact the company for clarification or open the packaging right in the store to inspect the operating instructions and any other paperwork contained within the packaging. (This is where you learn that you might as well, just stop trying to find anything made in the USA.) 

It should be required (I've seen it on some things) that the packaging, both inside a box and out, state the truth. If the item was assembled in China, but distributed from US warehouses, it should be clearly stated in a place where the potential buyer doesn't have to tear open packaging and root through the internal contents for the truth. The store owners don't like you to do that, however, I do it anyhow. 

Sad but true, usually there is no choice but to buy the Chinese made product because there just aren't that many things made in the US. At least if we knew up front what we were buying we could make an informed decision whether to continue with the purchase.

Thank you again for the opportunity to comment.

Despite public outcry and many consumer complaints, it is not at all obvious that loot boxes should be considered a form of gambling or that they represent a cause of serious harm. The main problem seems to revolve around a confusion among the gaming public between genuinely harmful products and products that are simply unappealing to consumers. Many gamers dislike loot box mechanics because they feel they disrupt the gameplay experience, especially by providing ways to unfairly unbalance competitive play by providing rewards that incentivise "pay-to-win" tactics. This frustration is understandable, but it is not equivalent to making the case for regulating game developers and their revenue models.

Much of the outcry over loot boxes consists of the same kind of moral panic that appears around practically every innovation in art or media, including radio, television, comic books, trading cards, board games, and virtually every original genre of music in the last century. And like those older innovations, loot boxes (and microtransactions in general) must be understood in their appropriate economic context. The economics of the game industry are changing rapidly and revenue models must evolve if the industry hopes to survive. Loot boxes are a case study of this kind of experimentation, and one that is still being played out. Crucially, we do not know whether consumers will ultimately decide for or against loot boxes.

Likewise, the existing academic literature on loot boxes and addictive behaviours, though well-intentioned, suffers from a wide range of problems relating to issues like choice of research methods and models, sampling, self-selection bias, and data interpretation. As a result, it does not provide a rationale for regulating loot boxes or for restricting their marketing or sale.

Furthermore, game developers and publishers, as well as industry trade associations and other stakeholders have demonstrated that they are taking the controversy seriously by modifying loot boxes to reduce or remove risk elements and by making draw rates transparent and/or more favourable to players. In several cases loot boxes have been removed completely from games. Parental warnings have also been updated and new educational initiatives have been launched by trade associations like the ESRB. Together, these examples show that self-regulation--which is really just a way of talking about how businesses try to satisfy customers by constantly updating their products--is active in the industry. A study of these self-regulatory efforts is available in a peer-reviewed paper titled, "The Macro Problem of Microtransactions: The Self-Regulatory Challenges of Video Game Loot Boxes" (see the attached file, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bushor.2019.03.001). A brief summary is also provided in the second attached file, which was submitted to the UK Parliamentary inquiry on Immersive and Addictive Technologies.
