To: FTC/Made in USA Workshop / Attn: Julia Ensor Solomon 
Re: Made in USA Claims, Project No. P074204

: Response to the request for public comment on guidelines for Made in USA:

I respectfully request that the unqualified claim for Made in USA as applied to the $50 Billion plus (per year) watch industry be made equal or similar to worldwide standards used by segment leaders including Swiss, Japanese, and Chinese/Hong Kong manufacturers. 

Swiss Made = 60% Swiss sourced component VALUE and final assembly in Switzerland for a finished watch. Domestic value factor is reduced to 50% for watch movements to be considered a Swiss watch movement. http://www.fhs.swiss/eng/strengthening.html

Made in Japan = Last major transformation of components to take place in Japan. No stipulated values. Industry estimates show nearly 50% of Japanese watches use majority Chinese components and partial assembly. 

Made in China/Hong Kong = No specific component values applied. Companies must be based in country. 

As our own American wristwatch industry begins a cycle of rebirth and reinvigoration, the US government is restricting the ability of domestic brands to compete with a crippling all or virtually all standard for an unqualified claim of Made in the USA. 

All or virtually all may be attainable for less complex products such as pillows or molded rubber floor mats, but with a complex product such as a wristwatch that can have 150 or more individual components; the existing standard is beyond crippling. It virtually eliminates the possibility to earn the esteemed status and benefits commensurate with an unqualified Made in USA status. 

Twenty two years ago a 75% value standard (plus final transformation) was proposed but never written into the FTC guidelines. https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/press-releases/1997/05/ftc-proposes-new-standard-made-usa-claims-seeks-public-comment 

Even this standard is substantially higher than any competitive member of the watch manufacturing countries, yet was never enacted. If we cannot play on a level playing field with the Swiss, Japanese, and Chinese, at least we should activate this reasonable guideline. 

I write this as both a 30 year veteran reporter on the watch industry and also as a recent entrant into the watch making arena here in the USA. With a growing list of over 200 American based watch brands I encourage a plan of action that will release the brakes on an industry that can train and employ thousands of Americans in the future. 

Thank you in advance for your kind attention.
Gary G. Girdvainis Editor-in-Chief iW Magazine, AboutTime Magazine / Isochron Media LLC

I have been in the Watch and Clock industry since 40 years. Having worked with top Swiss Watch Companies as a distributor and for manufacturing needs, the immense knowledge I have gained with regards to Swiss Made is invaluable. I write this as a consumer and also as a manufacturer of watches.The Swiss Made label is perceived globally as manufactured in Switzerland, although the swiss origin components amount to 30 - 40 percent or less. The 60 percent takes into consideration the cost of labor to assemble it. The 60 percent is based on the cost of the components and labor coming from Swiss origin. Yes the movement of the watch needs to be Swiss Made to qualify , however, the movement too is qualified as Swiss Made with 60 percent formula. Even the 60 percent is loosely controlled by swiss where watch industry is a major revenue earner, employer and exporter. I state this with valid personal experiences wherein I have manufactured numerous timepieces from Swiss vendors.

American watch brands desiring of manufacturing their watches in USA must get a level playing field to be able to compete the Swiss watch Brands in the domestic and world market. Consumers in China, Japan , India and many other countries are waiting to buy Made in USA watches . They know that Made in USA has stood for highest quality of product for over a century. 

American and global consumers have never questioned Swiss Made for decades and gladly accepted it as a mark of quality in the horological products. The well versed consumers too know that only 60 percent is swiss, but the perception is imbibed and accepted as Made in Switzerland.

There is no reason that the American and other global watch collectors and lovers of American Made goods will have any issue in accepting a genuine and true 60 percent qualification of Made in USA. Yes , the watch must use an American made movement or module with 60 percent content of USA origin. It is very important to have a level playing field , for the American watch brands who wish to Manufacture their timepieces in the USA and compete with Swiss with better value and superior American Technology.

Speaking strictly in regards to the U.S. watch industry, the Made in the USA designation has such restrictive and arduous rules for sourcing and manufacturing that it is absurd for almost any American watch brand attempting to obtain it. Most Americans are unaware that for 150 years America boasted a thriving and successful watch industry that employed thousands. We pioneered precision mass production, making reliable and accurate watches. However, by the 1960s American companies had gone out of business or had been bought out by foreign companies. The American watch industry has joined a long list of manufacturing sectors that have disappeared from the scene and with it millions of high paying, secure industrial jobs that had been built by the American middle class. The story of the long-lost American watch business is really the story of American manufacturing, with jobs and production gone overseas to save costs. While theres an increased demand from the consumer for American watches, the FTC restrictions place American watch brands at a distinct disadvantage with respect to our Swiss counterparts. The importance of American watches and the revival of the American watch industry cannot be overstated. Thanks to a renewed interest in American-made goods, a few smaller startup American watch brands are attempting to bring U.S. production back. While Switzerland and Asia are capable of churning out mechanical movements at scale and at low price points, America has not had the same kind of manufacturing support since the decline of the industry nearly 60 years ago, and revitalizing the industry has become the objective of quite a few companies in the past 5 years. More people are taking a moment to flip over an item or fish for a label and ask, is it Made in the USA? The biggest hurdle to the American watch industry may be that a new mind-set is needed we put men on the moon and three rovers on Mars, yet we cant see that we are competing in a global watch market worth $43 billion dollars which is Switzerland's 2nd largest sector, is 22% of their GDP and employs over 57,000 people? This is the most industrious nation in the world and the cynics are saying we can't do what the Swiss and Chinese are doing? The British and the Germans are doing it so surely we can do it. American companies are however at a disadvantage due to the stringent FTC requirements. If the clothier Patagonia can't achieve the label (https://www.patagonia.com/blog/2012/04/patagonia-clothing-made-where-how-why/) then what hope does a fledgling US watch company have?

Loot boxes are a blight on every game that implements them. They use slot machine like tactics to lure people in to paying for them. They exploit the risk/rewards systems of the brain, specifically the dopamine system. They are terrible for the consult and a cash cow for video game publishers and developers. Many games deliberately hinder progress if someone doesn't pay up. Many games are nearly unplayable because of them. If we don't put a complete end to loot boxes now, they will proliferate like weeds in a garden or an outbreak of Ebola.

Managing a children's game play is the parent's responsibility, as is teaching them the difference between imaginary and actual. Loot boxes are not the issue, parental responsibly is. I have am idea, tell your child that it doesn't matter, and help them develop their skills in other ways. I suspect many parents find that video games are cheaper than hiring a tutor, or entertaining the kids themselves.

Loot boxes can enhance gameplay when they are used as a fun way to get cosmetic items that do not have any impact on in game power. However, they are often used as a stealth pay wall:

1) Game play is often altered so that progression is tied to loot box luck rather than in game accomplishments (earning tokens to open loot boxes rather than actual items, for example)
2) Most have no mercy rule (guaranteed top prize after a set number of attempts to offset really bad luck...important since the odds of getting desired items are often lower than 1%). 
3) From my experience in free to play games that have loot boxes, the top players end up gambling thousands of dollars to make sure they have the best stuff. Those who dont pay sometimes get lucky, but usually dont stand a chance against those that do. 
4) Games often use tactics like always on PvP or tying important items for progression to PvP. 

In short, what could be a fun mechanic is often being abused to hold your progress ransom to dumb luck.

The problem I have with loot boxes and in-game purchases of coins/gems is this:
Often as a gamer you have 100's if not 1000's of hours invested in the game.
Then you buy a loot box or coins in-game. And it doesn't work. You try to work it out using these arcane in-game ticket systems but that fails, too. You've paid for this often using a credit card so you have recourse to complain about a purchase "not as described" or you simply never received it.
But here's the problem. They've totally got you and they know it. If you file a credit card charge complaint, they simply permanently ban you from the game. So as you have so much time and money invested already, you don't dare complain too much.
You have very few rights as a gamer. And some gaming companies are very unscrupulous, taking your money, making you think it's a great deal, and it's not, or you fail to get it, and then you have almost no recourse unless you want to lose everything you've put into the game. Games can ban you for any reason and often there is no right of appeal.

I have known people that had over ten years and thousands of hours in game, as well as thousands of dollars invested, only to lose everything due to some misunderstanding with customer service. And they have no recourse. They are just banned. They can't even email the game managers as you have to be in-game to do that. Trying to call them via phone or other contact methods are often impossible. In several cases I have personal information about, this game was that person's entire life. All their friends were in the game. Everyday they would be there, joyfully chatting with all their friends. And then some little thing happens, and the game executes it's terms of service and bans the person, and they commit suicide. This is an unseen and seldom discussed epidemic among gamers that have isolated themselves for years doing almost nothing in their life but playing a game, often they are disabled people who live alone, and when they complain about the loot box and get banned, they kill themselves. It's not a rare occurrence, although it doesn't happen often. They become addicted to the game and when that's suddenly turned off it's too much for them to bear. Playing Ultima Online for over 10 years when it first came out I knew one person who committed suicide after being banned. In playing Eve Online for over 10 years I knew several people who committed suicide, and there were rumors of others that I couldn't verify. At least two of these people were banned when they complained to customer service about issues with in-game purchases.
